name: Original Practice Test 1
source: Original LSAT-style questions written for LSAT Trainer (harder than the real test). Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Newspaper editor: Some reporters insist that granting anonymity to a source is justified whenever doing so yields a newsworthy story. They point out that many important exposés could not have been written otherwise. That is true, but it shows only that anonymity is sometimes warranted, not that it is warranted whenever a story is newsworthy. In fact, anonymity should be granted only as a last resort, when the information cannot be obtained in any other way. For anonymity shields sources from accountability for what they say, and readers cannot assess the credibility of a source they cannot identify.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: Many important exposés could not have been written without granting anonymity to sources.
That anonymity is sometimes warranted does not show that it is warranted whenever a story is newsworthy.
Anonymity should be granted to a source only when the information cannot be obtained in any other way.
Readers cannot assess the credibility of sources whose identities are withheld from them.
Reporters should rarely, if ever, pursue stories that depend on information from anonymous sources.
questions.explanation: The editor's position, supported by the final sentence about accountability and credibility, is that anonymity should be a last resort, which is (C). (B) is the tempting trap: it rebuts the reporters' evidence, but that rebuttal only clears the way for the editor's own claim and is not itself what the argument is ultimately trying to establish. (A) is the opponents' premise, which the editor concedes, and (E) overstates the editor's view.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Anonymity should be granted only as a last resort, when the information can't be obtained any other way.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Reporters' evidence (some exposés needed anonymity) only shows anonymity is sometimes warranted; anonymity shields sources from accountability; readers can't judge a source they can't identify.

breakdown.analysis: The editor does two things: knocks down the reporters' argument, then states her own view and supports it. The knock-down is a stepping stone. The thing she's ultimately selling is 'last resort only,' and the last sentence ('For...') is the support for exactly that. Quick test: ask 'why should I believe that?' about each candidate. Why only as a last resort? Because of accountability and credibility. That's the conclusion with its premise attached. Lesson: in main-conclusion questions, a rebuttal of the other side is usually a subsidiary step, not the main point.

choices.note: This is the reporters' evidence, which the editor concedes ('That is true'). A conceded premise from the other side is never the editor's conclusion.

The trap. It's a real claim the editor makes, but it only shows the reporters' evidence is too weak. It clears the ground for her actual position; it isn't the position itself. Nothing in the argument is offered to support (B) except the observation it already contains.

CORRECT. This is the 'In fact' sentence: anonymity only when the information can't be obtained otherwise. The final sentence ('For anonymity shields...') exists to support it, and it's the editor's own position on the issue.
This is a premise. It's offered as a reason for the last-resort rule, so it supports the conclusion rather than being it.
Too strong and off-topic. The editor talks about when to grant anonymity, not about avoiding stories that rely on anonymous sources. 'Last resort' isn't 'rarely, if ever pursue.'

questions.stimulus: Agricultural extension agent: Five years ago, sorghum accounted for 8 percent of the cropland in Corlan County; today it accounts for 14 percent. Sorghum tolerates drought far better than corn, the crop it has largely displaced, and the shift reflects a growing awareness among the county's farmers of the region's long-term water shortages. Clearly, then, more acres of sorghum are being planted in Corlan County today than were being planted five years ago.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: overlooks the possibility that the total amount of cropland in the county declined substantially over the five-year period
takes for granted that sorghum is more profitable for the county's farmers than corn is
presumes, without providing justification, that the shift toward sorghum will continue in future years
fails to consider that the average yield per acre of sorghum in the county may have fallen over the period
treats evidence about the proportion of farms that grow sorghum as though it were evidence about the proportion of cropland planted in it
questions.explanation: A rise in sorghum's share of cropland does not guarantee more sorghum acres, because total cropland may have shrunk; (A) identifies this percentage-versus-amount error. (D) is the trap: yield per acre has no bearing on how many acres are planted. (E) describes a confusion the argument never makes, since both figures concern cropland.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: More acres of sorghum are planted in Corlan County today than five years ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Sorghum's share of cropland rose from 8% to 14%; sorghum handles drought better than corn; farmers are reacting to water shortages.

breakdown.analysis: Classic percentage-versus-amount flaw. A bigger slice doesn't mean a bigger amount if the pie shrank. Concretely: 8% of 1,000 acres is 80 acres; 14% of 500 acres is 70 acres. The share went up and the acreage went down. The drought story is just color; it doesn't fix the math. Lesson: whenever an argument jumps from a percentage to a raw number (or back), ask what happened to the total.

choices.note: CORRECT. If total cropland shrank enough, 14% of the new total can be fewer acres than 8% of the old total. That's exactly the gap between 'share rose' and 'acres rose.'
The argument never relies on profitability. It explains the shift through drought tolerance, and the conclusion is about acreage, not why farmers chose sorghum.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Farmers here are switching to sorghum, so sorghum must make them more money than corn.

choices.note: The conclusion is about today versus five years ago. Nothing is said or assumed about future years.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Sorghum's share has grown for five years, so it will keep growing for the next five.

choices.note: The trap, because it sounds like a quantity issue. But yield per acre is about how much grain each acre produces, not how many acres are planted. The conclusion is strictly about acres.
The argument never mentions the proportion of farms. Both the premise and the conclusion are about cropland, so there's no farms-versus-cropland confusion.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: 30% of farms grow sorghum, so sorghum must cover 30% of the cropland.

questions.stimulus: Three years ago, public health authorities in the city of Marbury launched a campaign urging adult residents to have their skin examined for cancer once a year, and participation in such screenings has since tripled. Over the same period, the number of new skin cancer cases diagnosed each year in Marbury has risen sharply. Yet the number of Marbury residents who die of skin cancer each year has declined steadily since the campaign began.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The screening campaign was paid for by a grant that is scheduled to expire next year.
Diagnosed cases of skin cancer have also risen in several cities that have conducted no screening campaigns.
Most of the Marbury residents who were screened had no family history of skin cancer.
Some forms of skin cancer are considerably more dangerous than other forms.
Screening detects many skin cancers that would otherwise have gone unnoticed until a later stage, when they are far harder to treat successfully.
questions.explanation: (E) explains both facts: screening finds more cancers, raising the number of diagnoses, and finds them early, when treatment works better, lowering deaths. (B) is the trap: it offers a reason diagnoses might rise everywhere but does nothing to explain why deaths in Marbury fell.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Since the screening campaign began, new skin cancer diagnoses in Marbury have risen sharply, but skin cancer deaths have steadily declined.

breakdown.analysis: More cancer found, fewer cancer deaths. The prephrase practically writes itself: screening finds cancers that would have been missed (so diagnoses go up) and finds them early, when they're treatable (so deaths go down). It's like a mechanic doing more inspections: he finds more problems, but fewer cars break down on the highway. The right answer needs to explain both halves, especially the falling deaths.

choices.note: Funding expiring next year says nothing about what happened over the past three years. Irrelevant.

The trap. It might suggest diagnoses are rising for some general reason, but it does nothing to explain the hard part: why deaths in Marbury fell. If anything, it makes the screening look less responsible for the diagnosis jump.
Family history of the people screened doesn't connect diagnoses to deaths. It doesn't explain why more cases led to fewer deaths.
True of most diseases and useless here. It doesn't say the dangerous forms became less common or got caught earlier, so it explains neither trend.

CORRECT. Screening catches many cancers that would otherwise go unnoticed (diagnoses up) and catches them before the stage where they're hard to treat (deaths down). Both facts now make sense together.

questions.stimulus: Music school director: Students in our program who use a metronome for at least half of their practice time score markedly higher on our rhythmic-accuracy assessments than do students who rarely or never use one. Therefore, to improve our students' rhythmic accuracy, we should require every student in the program to practice with a metronome for at least half of the time they spend practicing.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Some of the students who practice with a metronome also take private lessons outside the program.
Students who already have strong rhythmic skills find metronome practice far less frustrating than other students do and so are much more likely to choose it.
Rhythmic-accuracy assessments are only one of several measures the school uses to evaluate its students.
Metronomes are inexpensive and are available as free applications for most phones.
Many professional musicians report that they regularly practiced with a metronome when they were students.
questions.explanation: (B) suggests the correlation runs the other way: students with good rhythm choose the metronome, rather than the metronome producing good rhythm, so requiring it may not help. (A) mentions an alternative factor but only for 'some' students, which is far too weak to undermine the comparison.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Requiring all students to use a metronome for at least half their practice would improve rhythmic accuracy.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Students who use a metronome at least half the time score much higher on rhythm assessments than students who rarely or never do.

breakdown.analysis: Correlation-to-causation. The director assumes the metronome causes better rhythm. The classic way to weaken this is reverse causation or a third factor. Maybe students who already have good rhythm are the ones who like metronomes. It's like noticing that people at the gym are fit and concluding the gym made them fit; maybe fit people are just the ones who go. If that's what's happening, forcing everyone onto a metronome won't make them better.

choices.note: An alternative factor (private lessons), but only for 'some' metronome users, and we don't know whether non-users also take lessons. Way too weak to explain a marked difference.

CORRECT. Reverse causation: good rhythm leads students to choose the metronome, not the other way around. That explains the correlation without the metronome doing anything, so requiring it may not help.
The argument is only about rhythmic accuracy. That the school uses other measures too doesn't touch whether metronomes improve this one.
Cost and availability matter to whether the rule is practical, not to whether it would improve rhythm. If anything it removes an objection.
Professionals used metronomes as students; this, if anything, slightly supports the idea that metronomes go with skill. It doesn't weaken.

questions.stimulus:
Ilsa: The Kerrow Observatory should replace its aging optical telescope with a radio telescope. Radio observations are unaffected by the cloud cover that prevents optical observing on most nights at Kerrow, so a radio instrument would yield far more usable data for the same cost.

Tomas: Admittedly, a radio telescope would gather more data. But the observatory's principal mission is public education, and visitors come to Kerrow to look through an eyepiece at the planets and stars. A radio telescope offers nothing of that kind, so replacing the optical telescope with one would undermine the observatory's mission.
questions.stem: Ilsa and Tomas disagree over whether
choices: a radio telescope would yield more usable data than the optical telescope does
cloud cover prevents optical observing on most nights at Kerrow
public education is the principal mission of the Kerrow Observatory
the Kerrow Observatory should replace its optical telescope with a radio telescope
visitors would continue to come to Kerrow if it had no optical telescope
questions.explanation: Ilsa says the observatory should make the replacement and Tomas says doing so would undermine its mission, so they disagree about (D). Tomas explicitly concedes (A), and neither speaker takes a position on both sides of (B), (C), or (E).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ilsa: Kerrow should replace its optical telescope with a radio telescope because radio gets far more usable data despite clouds.; Tomas: A radio telescope would get more data, but the observatory's mission is public education, so the replacement would undermine that mission.

breakdown.analysis: Ilsa says 'replace it.' Tomas concedes the data point but says replacing it undermines the mission, which is clearly a 'no, don't.' Lesson: to disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Check each answer by asking 'what would Ilsa say? what would Tomas say?' If either has no opinion, or they agree, it's out.

choices.note: Tomas explicitly agrees ('Admittedly, a radio telescope would gather more data'). Both say yes, so no disagreement.
Ilsa asserts it; Tomas never addresses cloud cover at all. One opinion isn't a disagreement.
Tomas asserts public education is the principal mission; Ilsa says nothing about the mission. No position from her, so no disagreement.
CORRECT. Ilsa: yes, replace it. Tomas: replacing it would undermine the mission, so no. That's a clean yes/no split.
Tomas hints visitors come to look through an eyepiece, but never says they'd stop coming, and Ilsa says nothing about visitors. Neither speaker clearly commits.

questions.stimulus: Economist: The province of Velmont is considering a law that would require employers to give hourly workers at least two weeks' notice of their work schedules. Opponents claim the law would impose heavy costs on Velmont's businesses. But a nearly identical law took effect in the neighboring province of Arden four years ago, and Arden's businesses have reported no significant increase in operating costs since then. So the proposed law would not impose heavy costs on Velmont's businesses.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Velmont's businesses do not rely on last-minute changes to workers' schedules to a much greater extent than Arden's businesses do.
Operating costs for Arden's businesses would have declined over the past four years had the law not taken effect.
Most hourly workers in Velmont are in favor of the proposed law.
Arden's law has been enforced without exception since it took effect.
No business in Arden has incurred any expense in complying with the scheduling law.
questions.explanation: The argument relies on Arden being a good model for Velmont; if Velmont's businesses depended far more on last-minute scheduling, Arden's experience would say little about Velmont, so (A) is required. (D) is tempting, but the argument does not need perfect enforcement, and (E) is far stronger than the claim that costs are not heavy.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Velmont's proposed scheduling law would not impose heavy costs on Velmont's businesses.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A nearly identical law in Arden took effect four years ago; Arden's businesses reported no significant increase in operating costs.

breakdown.analysis: This is an analogy argument: it worked fine in Arden, so it'll work fine in Velmont. Any analogy argument assumes the two cases are alike in the ways that matter. It's like saying 'my brother handled this diet fine, so you will too' when you might be diabetic. For this law, the key difference would be how much businesses depend on short-notice scheduling. Use the negation test: negate each answer and see if the argument falls apart.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: Velmont's businesses rely on last-minute schedule changes much more than Arden's. Then Arden's easy experience tells us nothing about Velmont, and the argument collapses. So it's required.
choices.negation: Velmont's businesses DO rely on last-minute schedule changes to a much greater extent than Arden's businesses do.

choices.note: Negate it: costs would NOT have declined without the law. That's the boring normal case and doesn't hurt the argument at all. (The original version would actually suggest the law had a hidden cost, so it's closer to a weakener.)
choices.negation: Operating costs for Arden's businesses would not have declined over the past four years had the law not taken effect.

choices.note: Negate it: most hourly workers in Velmont aren't in favor. Workers' opinions say nothing about business costs. No effect.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most hourly workers in Velmont favor the proposed law.

choices.note: Tempting, but negate it: there were some exceptions in enforcement. If the law was mostly enforced, Arden is still decent evidence. The argument doesn't need perfect enforcement, so negating it doesn't kill the argument.
choices.negation: Arden's law has not been enforced without exception; there has been at least one exception.

choices.note: Far too strong. Negate it: at least one Arden business had some compliance expense. That's perfectly consistent with costs not being 'heavy.' No damage.
choices.negation: At least one business in Arden has incurred some expense in complying with the law.

questions.stimulus: Pottery fragments recovered from the lowest occupation layer at the Tessin Hill site are decorated with a distinctive cord-impressed pattern. In the surrounding region, that pattern has been found at only one other site, Varro Creek, forty kilometers away, and radiocarbon dating shows that the Varro Creek pottery is at least two centuries older than any pottery found at Tessin Hill. Archaeologists agree that the cord-impressed technique is far too intricate to have been invented independently at more than one place in the region.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: People from Varro Creek eventually migrated to Tessin Hill and settled there.
The cord-impressed pattern was the most common form of pottery decoration at Varro Creek.
The cord-impressed technique used on the Tessin Hill pottery probably did not originate at Tessin Hill.
No pottery made anywhere in the region before the Varro Creek pottery bore a cord-impressed pattern.
The inhabitants of Tessin Hill obtained their pottery by trading with the inhabitants of Varro Creek.
questions.explanation: Since the technique was not invented twice in the region and older examples exist at Varro Creek, the Tessin Hill potters very likely learned it from elsewhere, supporting (C). (A) and (E) name one specific means of transmission that the evidence does not single out, and (D) makes a claim about all pottery in the region, including pottery not yet discovered.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Lowest-layer Tessin Hill pottery has a distinctive cord-impressed pattern; 2) the only other regional site with it is Varro Creek; 3) Varro Creek's pottery is at least two centuries older than any at Tessin Hill; 4) the technique is too intricate to have been invented independently more than once in the region.

breakdown.analysis: Put facts 3 and 4 together. If the technique was only invented once in the region, and Varro Creek had it centuries earlier, then Tessin Hill almost certainly didn't invent it. It came from somewhere else. But how it got there (migration, trade, a traveling potter) is not specified. Lesson: the supported answer goes as far as the facts and no further.

choices.note: Migration is one possible way the technique spread, but so are trade or intermarriage. You can't pick an answer on a possibility.
We know Varro Creek had the pattern, not how common it was compared to other decorations there. Nothing supports 'most common.'
CORRECT. Invented only once in the region, and older examples exist elsewhere, so the Tessin Hill potters most likely didn't originate it. 'Probably' keeps it appropriately modest.
Too strong. We only know about pottery found so far; some older, undiscovered pottery anywhere in the region could have the pattern. 'No pottery made anywhere' goes way past the evidence.
Like (A), it picks one specific transmission story. The Tessin Hill people might have made the pottery themselves after learning the technique. Unsupported.

questions.stimulus: Consumer advocate: Advertisers accused of deceiving the public often defend their campaigns by pointing out that every statement in them is literally true. But literal truth is not enough to protect consumers, who reasonably draw conclusions from what an advertisement suggests as well as from what it says. An advertisement is misleading if it implies that the advertised product provides a benefit that the product has not been shown to provide, regardless of whether each individual statement in the advertisement is accurate.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: An advertisement for Glisten toothpaste is not misleading, because the only claim it makes, that Glisten contains fluoride, is true.
An advertisement for Corvin running shoes is misleading, because its claim that the shoes weigh less than 200 grams is false.
An advertisement for Pellam vitamins is misleading, because it was produced by an agency whose previous campaigns were widely criticized.
An advertisement for Hartwell soup is not misleading, because the benefit it implies, lower cholesterol, has been demonstrated in a study.
An advertisement for Brisa tea is misleading: it accurately says Brisa contains antioxidants, but it implies that drinking Brisa prevents illness, which has never been demonstrated.
questions.explanation: (E) matches the principle exactly: the ad implies an undemonstrated benefit, so it is misleading even though its statement is accurate. (A) and (D) conclude that ads are not misleading, but the principle gives only a condition sufficient for being misleading, not one for avoiding that label; (B) concerns a false statement, which the principle does not address.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: If an ad implies the product provides a benefit that hasn't been shown → the ad is misleading (even if every statement is literally true).

breakdown.analysis: The principle gives one sufficient condition for 'misleading': implied, undemonstrated benefit → misleading. It does not tell you when an ad is NOT misleading. So any answer concluding 'not misleading' can't be justified by this rule, and any answer concluding 'misleading' must be based on an implied, unproven benefit. Lesson: a sufficient condition tells you what to conclude when it's met, and nothing when it isn't.

choices.note: Concludes 'not misleading.' The principle never gives conditions for that. A true claim isn't enough; that's exactly the defense the advocate rejects.
Concludes 'misleading,' but because a statement is false. The principle is about implied, unproven benefits, not false statements.
The agency's reputation is irrelevant to the principle. Nothing about an implied benefit.
Another 'not misleading' conclusion. Failing the trigger (benefit was demonstrated) doesn't let you conclude the opposite. That's the mistaken negation of a conditional.

CORRECT. The statement (contains antioxidants) is accurate, but the ad implies preventing illness, a benefit never demonstrated. Trigger met, so 'misleading' follows, and the answer even matches the 'regardless of accuracy' part.

questions.stimulus: Media critic: The Ledger insists that its reporters' coverage of elections is never influenced by their personal political views. Yet an anonymous survey conducted last year found that a large majority of the Ledger's political reporters regularly vote for candidates of the same party. Clearly, then, the Ledger's election coverage is biased in favor of that party, whatever the paper's editors may claim.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: relies on a survey whose respondents may not have been representative of the Ledger's political reporters
treats a characteristic of the people who produce something as conclusive evidence of a characteristic of what they produce
attacks the motives of the Ledger's editors rather than addressing the substance of their claim
concludes that a claim is true merely because it has not been shown to be false
infers from the fact that most of the Ledger's political reporters share a preference that all of them share it
questions.explanation: The critic moves from the reporters having a party preference (a feature of the producers) to the coverage being biased (a feature of the product), assuming the preference shapes the work; (B) describes this abstractly. (E) is the trap: the conclusion does not require every reporter to share the preference, and nothing suggests the survey sample in (A) was unrepresentative.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Ledger's election coverage is biased in favor of one party.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A survey found most of the Ledger's political reporters regularly vote for that party's candidates.

breakdown.analysis: The critic jumps from what the reporters believe to what the coverage says. That's a gap: people can hold views and still do neutral work. It's like saying a referee who's a Lakers fan must have called the game unfairly, without looking at a single call. The flaw is treating a trait of the producers as proof of a trait of the product.

choices.note: Nothing suggests the survey was unrepresentative; it was of the Ledger's political reporters. Describes a flaw the argument doesn't commit.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Ten readers who wrote angry letters hate the new layout, so most of our readers must hate it.

choices.note: CORRECT. The reporters' voting preference (a feature of the producers) is treated as conclusive proof that the coverage (the product) is biased. The argument never examines the coverage itself.
The critic doesn't attack the editors' motives; she just says their claim is wrong because of the survey. No ad hominem here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The editors say coverage is fair, but they'd say anything to protect their circulation, so the coverage must be biased.

choices.note: The argument cites positive evidence (the survey); it doesn't say 'no one has proven otherwise.'
choices.example: Example of flaw: No one has shown the Ledger is unbiased, so it must be biased.

choices.note: The trap. The argument says 'a large majority,' and its conclusion about biased coverage doesn't need every reporter to share the preference. It never makes the most-to-all leap.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Most Ledger reporters vote for Party X, so every Ledger reporter does.

questions.stimulus: Agricultural researcher: In the Dunmore Valley, apple orchards bordered by hedgerows of native wildflowers have suffered far less damage from codling moths than orchards without such borders. The wildflowers attract parasitic wasps, which lay their eggs inside codling moth larvae, killing them. Therefore, planting native wildflower hedgerows along the Dunmore Valley orchards that currently lack them would reduce codling moth damage in those orchards.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Wildflower-bordered orchards in the valley contain more of the parasitic wasps than do orchards without such borders.
Codling moths cause more damage than any other insect pest in the Dunmore Valley's orchards.
Orchards with wildflower hedgerows are, on average, located at higher elevations, where codling moths are less common.
In valley orchards where wildflower hedgerows were planted only recently, codling moth damage fell within two seasons to the levels seen in orchards with long-established hedgerows.
Most owners of valley orchards that lack hedgerows have said they are unwilling to plant them.
questions.explanation: The argument infers from a correlation that adding hedgerows would cut damage; (D) shows that when orchards gained hedgerows, their own damage fell, which rules out preexisting differences between orchards as the explanation. (A) is the most tempting trap, but it merely repeats the premise that wildflowers attract wasps and does not address whether other differences explain the lower damage. (E) is irrelevant to a conditional conclusion, and (C) weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Planting wildflower hedgerows along Dunmore Valley orchards that lack them would reduce codling moth damage there.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Hedgerow orchards suffer far less moth damage than others; wildflowers attract wasps that kill moth larvae.

breakdown.analysis: The evidence is a comparison between two existing groups of orchards. The conclusion is a prediction: add hedgerows and damage drops. The worry is that hedgerow orchards differ in some other way (location, management, climate). Best strengthener: show that adding hedgerows actually changed things in the same orchards. It's like proving a tutor helps by showing the same student's scores went up after starting tutoring, not just that tutored kids score higher.

choices.note: The most tempting trap. It mostly restates the mechanism the argument already gives (wildflowers attract wasps). It doesn't rule out other differences between the two sets of orchards that might explain the damage gap.
Tells us moths are a big problem, which makes the conclusion important, not more likely to be true.
This weakens. Elevation is an alternative explanation for why hedgerow orchards have less damage.

CORRECT. Orchards that added hedgerows saw damage fall to the levels of long-established hedgerow orchards. That's a before-and-after in the same orchards, which knocks out 'they were different all along' and supports the prediction.
Whether owners are willing to plant is irrelevant to what would happen if they did. The conclusion is conditional.

questions.stimulus: Some astronomers attribute the faint, regular dimming of the star Corvan-7 to an orbiting planet that periodically passes in front of it. But the dimming is better explained by an orbiting cloud of dust. A planet large enough to produce dimming of the observed magnitude would exert a gravitational tug on Corvan-7, causing a detectable wobble in the star's position, yet repeated precise measurements have revealed no such wobble. It is therefore unlikely that any planet of that size orbits Corvan-7. A dust cloud, by contrast, could block that much starlight while exerting no noticeable gravitational pull.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that it is unlikely that any planet of that size orbits Corvan-7?
choices: It is the overall conclusion of the argument.
It is a concession to the astronomers whose explanation the argument rejects.
It is an observation that the competing explanations are each intended to account for.
It is a premise offered in support of the claim that a dust cloud could block starlight without exerting a noticeable gravitational pull.
It is a conclusion drawn from other statements in the argument and used in turn to support the argument's main conclusion.
questions.explanation: The claim is inferred ('therefore') from the wobble premises and then helps establish the main conclusion, stated in the second sentence, that a dust cloud better explains the dimming; so (E) is correct. (A) is the trap set by the word 'therefore', but the argument's ultimate point is the dust-cloud explanation. (D) misidentifies what the claim supports: the dust cloud's lack of gravitational pull is asserted independently.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The dimming of Corvan-7 is better explained by an orbiting dust cloud than by a planet.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A planet big enough to cause the dimming would cause a detectable wobble; no wobble has been found; so a planet that size is unlikely (intermediate conclusion); a dust cloud could block the light without noticeable gravity.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: wobble facts → 'unlikely that a planet that size orbits' → dust cloud is the better explanation. The claim in question has support coming in (the wobble evidence, signaled by 'therefore') and support going out (it knocks out the planet theory, helping the dust cloud win). That's an intermediate conclusion. Lesson: 'therefore' marks a conclusion, but not necessarily the main one. Always ask what the whole argument is trying to prove.

choices.note: The trap set by 'therefore.' But the argument's main point, stated up front with 'But,' is that the dust cloud is the better explanation. This claim serves that point.
It's not a concession; it's the opposite of what the planet astronomers believe. It attacks their view.
The observation both explanations try to account for is the dimming, not the absence of a large planet.
The dust cloud's lack of gravitational pull is simply asserted on its own. The planet claim doesn't support it; both support the main conclusion side by side.
CORRECT. It's inferred from the wobble premises ('therefore') and then used to rule out the planet, supporting the main conclusion that a dust cloud better explains the dimming.

questions.stimulus: Labor relations officer: At Halvorsen Manufacturing, no worker is certified to operate the heavy presses unless he or she has completed the advanced safety course. Every worker who completed that course last year is certified to operate the heavy presses, and workers certified to operate the heavy presses are never assigned to the packaging line. Dana Okafor, a Halvorsen worker, completed the advanced safety course last year. It follows that Dana is not eligible for this quarter's productivity bonus.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Only workers assigned to the packaging line are eligible for this quarter's productivity bonus.
Every worker assigned to the packaging line is eligible for this quarter's productivity bonus.
Any worker who is not certified to operate the heavy presses is assigned to the packaging line.
No worker who has completed the advanced safety course is eligible for this quarter's productivity bonus unless certified to operate the heavy presses.
Every worker eligible for this quarter's productivity bonus has completed the advanced safety course.
questions.explanation: The premises establish that Dana is certified and therefore not on the packaging line; (A) says eligibility requires being on the packaging line, so Dana is ineligible. (B) reverses that conditional, and (D) is the subtle trap: it states a requirement Dana already meets (certification), so it cannot rule her out. (E) builds on the irrelevant first premise and is consistent with Dana being eligible.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Dana is not eligible for this quarter's productivity bonus.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Certified → completed course; completed course last year → certified; certified → not on packaging line; Dana completed the course last year.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it for Dana: completed course last year → certified → NOT on packaging line. So we know Dana is not on the packaging line. We need: not on packaging line → not eligible. Contrapositive: eligible → on packaging line. That's 'only packaging-line workers are eligible.' The first premise (certified → course) is a distraction; it runs the wrong way to help.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Only packaging-line workers are eligible' means eligible → packaging line. Contrapositive: not on packaging line → not eligible. Dana isn't on the packaging line, so she's not eligible. Conclusion locked.
Reversal. Packaging line → eligible tells you about people on the line. Dana isn't on the line, and this says nothing about people off it.
Not certified → packaging line. Dana is certified, so this doesn't apply to her and tells us nothing about eligibility anyway.
The subtle trap. Completed course AND eligible → certified. Dana completed the course and IS certified, so she meets the requirement. It can't rule her out.
Eligible → completed course. Dana completed the course, so this is consistent with her being eligible. It actually leaves the door open, the opposite of what we need.

questions.stimulus: Health official: Two years ago, the town of Brennick imposed a tax on sugar-sweetened beverages sold within town limits, with the aim of reducing residents' consumption of such drinks. Since the tax took effect, sales of sugar-sweetened beverages in Brennick's stores have fallen by 30 percent, while sales of bottled water there have risen. Thus, the tax has substantially reduced Brennick residents' consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: whether the revenue raised by the tax has been spent on public health programs
whether sugar-sweetened beverages are the largest source of added sugar in Brennick residents' diets
whether Brennick residents have increased their purchases of sugar-sweetened beverages from stores outside the town since the tax took effect
whether other towns in the region are considering adopting similar taxes
whether the tax was supported by a majority of Brennick's voters when it was enacted
questions.explanation: The argument infers lower consumption from lower in-town sales; if residents simply buy the drinks in neighboring towns, consumption may not have fallen, so the answer to (C) bears directly on the argument. (B) concerns the health significance of these drinks, not whether consumption declined.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The tax has substantially reduced Brennick residents' consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the tax, sales of sugary drinks in Brennick's stores fell 30%; bottled water sales there rose.

breakdown.analysis: The evidence is about sales in Brennick's stores. The conclusion is about what Brennick residents drink. Those aren't the same thing. If residents just drive to the next town and stock up there, in-town sales drop but consumption doesn't. It's like concluding someone quit coffee because they stopped buying it at the office cafe, when they now bring a thermos from home. For evaluate questions, find the question whose answer would swing the argument either way.

choices.note: Where the revenue goes is a policy question. It doesn't tell us whether consumption actually fell.
Tempting because it sounds health-related, but the LSAT is ultra specific: the argument is about whether consumption of these drinks fell, not how important they are to residents' sugar intake.

CORRECT. If residents are buying more sugary drinks outside town, the in-town sales drop overstates (or fakes) the decline in consumption, and the argument weakens. If they aren't, the sales data looks like a good proxy, and the argument strengthens. Either answer matters.
What other towns plan to do has no bearing on what happened in Brennick.
Popularity of the tax when it passed tells us nothing about its effect on consumption.

questions.stimulus: At the Larkspur Conservatory, every student in the advanced composition seminar has studied counterpoint, and most students who have studied counterpoint have also studied orchestration. No student who has studied orchestration is a member of the conservatory's jazz ensemble unless that student has also studied improvisation. Every member of the jazz ensemble has studied counterpoint, but none of the ensemble's members has studied improvisation.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Some students in the advanced composition seminar have studied orchestration.
Most students who have studied counterpoint are not members of the jazz ensemble.
No member of the jazz ensemble is enrolled in the advanced composition seminar.
Most students who have studied orchestration have also studied counterpoint.
Every student who has studied improvisation has also studied orchestration.
questions.explanation: A jazz ensemble member who had studied orchestration would have to have studied improvisation, but none has, so no ensemble member has studied orchestration; since most counterpoint students have studied orchestration, most counterpoint students are outside the ensemble, which is (B). (A) is the trap: seminar students are only some of the counterpoint students and could all fall in the minority who never studied orchestration. (D) reverses the 'most' relationship.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Seminar → counterpoint; 2) most counterpoint students → orchestration; 3) orchestration AND jazz → improvisation; 4) jazz → counterpoint; 5) jazz → NOT improvisation.

breakdown.analysis: Combine 3 and 5. A jazz member who'd studied orchestration would need improvisation, but no jazz member has it. So jazz → NOT orchestration. Now fact 2: most counterpoint students studied orchestration, and none of those can be in jazz. So most counterpoint students are not in jazz. Imagine 100 counterpoint students: at least 51 took orchestration, and all 51 are barred from the ensemble.

choices.note: The trap. Seminar students are a subset of counterpoint students, and the 'most' could be entirely outside the seminar. Every seminar student could be in the minority who skipped orchestration. Possible, not required.

CORRECT. Jazz → not orchestration (since orchestration jazz members would need improvisation, which none have). Most counterpoint students have orchestration, so that majority is outside the jazz ensemble.
Nothing prevents overlap. A jazz member who has counterpoint but no orchestration could also sit in the seminar.

Reverses the 'most.' Most counterpoint students took orchestration; that says nothing about what share of orchestration students took counterpoint. There could be tons of orchestration students without counterpoint.
Improvisation only shows up as a requirement for orchestration students in jazz. Nothing says improvisation students must have orchestration.

questions.stimulus: Marketing director: Last year we replaced the plain brown box of our Orchard Crisp crackers with a brightly colored one, and in the following months Orchard Crisp's monthly sales rose 18 percent. Our Seaside Wheat crackers are sold in the same stores and still come in a plain brown box. So if we give Seaside Wheat brightly colored packaging as well, its sales are likely to rise substantially.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Seaside Wheat has historically sold fewer boxes per month than Orchard Crisp has.
Total cracker sales in the stores that carry both brands rose by about 2 percent over the same period.
Customers surveyed after the redesign said that they found the new Orchard Crisp box appealing.
Nearly all Seaside Wheat purchases are planned repeat purchases by customers who seek out the brand, whereas most Orchard Crisp purchases are made on impulse at the shelf.
Brightly colored packaging costs slightly more to produce than plain brown packaging does.
questions.explanation: The argument assumes Seaside Wheat would respond to packaging as Orchard Crisp did; (D) shows a relevant difference, since eye-catching packaging matters for impulse purchases but little for buyers who already seek out a brand. (B) is the trap: a general rise in cracker sales would weaken the argument only if it were large enough to account for the 18 percent increase, and 2 percent is not. (C) tends to strengthen.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Giving Seaside Wheat brightly colored packaging will likely raise its sales substantially.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Orchard Crisp's sales rose 18% after it switched to a bright box; Seaside Wheat is sold in the same stores and still has a plain brown box.

breakdown.analysis: Analogy argument: it worked for Orchard Crisp, so it'll work for Seaside Wheat. To weaken, find a relevant difference between the two products. Bright packaging works by grabbing someone at the shelf. If Seaside Wheat buyers already know what they want before they walk in, the box hardly matters. It's like redesigning the cover of a textbook students are required to buy: nobody's choosing it for the cover.

choices.note: A difference, but not one that matters to whether packaging boosts sales. A smaller brand could still see a big percentage jump.
The trap. A general market rise could explain some of Orchard Crisp's jump, but 2% is nowhere near 18%. The packaging still looks like it did most of the work.
Customers liked the new box. That supports the idea that packaging drove sales, so it strengthens.

CORRECT. Orchard Crisp sells on impulse, where eye-catching packaging matters. Seaside Wheat sells to planned repeat buyers who seek out the brand, where packaging matters little. The analogy breaks down.
A slight cost increase affects profit, not whether sales would rise. The conclusion is about sales.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Some critics say that newspapers should never publish photographs of people in grief, because doing so intrudes on private suffering. But had newspapers consistently followed that rule, they could not have published the photographs of famine victims in the Selva region that, decades ago, moved readers to fund an international relief effort that saved many thousands of lives. A rule that would have prevented such an outcome is not one that newspapers should adopt without qualification.
questions.stem: The columnist's argument proceeds by
choices: arguing that a rule should be rejected entirely because applying it would produce at least one undesirable result
showing that a proposed rule, if applied consistently, would have ruled out an action whose consequences were clearly desirable
offering a counterexample to show that a general claim about newspapers' past practices is inaccurate
appealing to the authority of experts in journalism ethics to discredit a proposed rule
inferring that because a practice once had good results, it will always have good results
questions.explanation: The columnist shows that the critics' rule would have blocked the famine photographs, whose effects were clearly good, which is (B). (A) is the closest trap but is too strong: the columnist concludes only that the rule should not be adopted 'without qualification,' not that it should be rejected entirely. (C) is wrong because the famine case counters a proposed rule, not a claim about what newspapers have done.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Newspapers shouldn't adopt, without qualification, a rule against publishing photos of people in grief.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Under that rule, the Selva famine photos couldn't have been published; those photos sparked a relief effort that saved thousands of lives.

breakdown.analysis: The columnist takes the critics' proposed rule, applies it to a real past case, and shows it would have blocked something clearly good. That's a counterexample to the rule's wisdom, and note the modest conclusion: not 'reject the rule,' just 'don't adopt it without qualification.' Lesson: in method questions, match the strength of the conclusion exactly.

choices.note: The closest trap, but too strong. The columnist says the rule shouldn't be adopted 'without qualification,' not that it should be rejected entirely.
choices.example: Example of this method: A ban on fireworks would have stopped one lovely festival, so we should throw out any limits on fireworks.

choices.note: CORRECT. The rule, applied consistently, would have ruled out publishing the famine photos, and the consequences of publishing (thousands of lives saved) were clearly desirable. That's precisely the move.
The critics' claim is a proposed rule about what newspapers should do, not a general claim about what they did in the past. The famine case challenges a rule, not a historical generalization.
choices.example: Example of this method: Critics say newspapers have never run grief photos. But the Selva photos were exactly that, so the critics are wrong.

choices.note: No experts are cited. The columnist argues from a historical case, not from authority.
choices.example: Example of this method: Leading journalism ethicists reject the critics' rule, so newspapers shouldn't adopt it.

choices.note: The columnist doesn't say publishing grief photos will always turn out well; she just says one case shows the rule is too blunt.
choices.example: Example of this method: Running grief photos once saved thousands of lives, so running them will always do good.

questions.stimulus: Science writer: Astronomers classify a supernova as 'nearby' if it occurs anywhere within our own galaxy, and they expect a nearby supernova, in this sense, to occur roughly once a century. Studies indicate that a nearby supernova—say, one within a few dozen light-years of the solar system—would bathe Earth in radiation intense enough to strip away much of the ozone layer. Therefore, Earth's ozone layer faces a serious threat from a supernova roughly once a century.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes that an event expected roughly once a century will occur exactly once in each century
takes for granted that the loss of much of the ozone layer would be harmful to life on Earth
confuses a condition sufficient for loss of the ozone layer with a condition necessary for it
relies on expectations that may be based on observations of galaxies other than our own
uses a term in one sense in one premise and in a much narrower sense in another premise while treating the two senses as equivalent
questions.explanation: 'Nearby' means anywhere in the galaxy in the first premise but within a few dozen light-years in the second, and the conclusion requires treating them as the same; (E) names this equivocation. (C) is tempting because the argument involves a condition for ozone loss, but the problem is not a necessary-sufficient reversal, and (A) fails because the conclusion itself says only 'roughly' once a century.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Earth's ozone layer faces a serious threat from a supernova roughly once a century.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 'Nearby' supernovas (anywhere in our galaxy) occur about once a century; a 'nearby' supernova (within a few dozen light-years) would strip much of the ozone layer.

breakdown.analysis: Watch the word 'nearby.' First it means anywhere in the galaxy, which is enormous. Then it means within a few dozen light-years, which is a tiny neighborhood. The once-a-century rate applies to the broad sense; the ozone damage applies to the narrow sense. Gluing them together is equivocation. It's like saying 'local' restaurants (anywhere in the state) open weekly, and a 'local' restaurant (on your block) would make your street noisy, so your street gets noisier every week.

choices.note: The conclusion itself says 'roughly' once a century, so the argument doesn't presume exactly once per century.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Floods here happen about once a decade, and we had one in 2021, so there won't be another until 2031.

choices.note: Even granting the ozone loss is harmful, the problem remains: the frequency doesn't apply to the dangerous kind of supernova. And 'serious threat' is reasonable if much of the ozone is stripped.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The storm will knock out the town's power, so it will clearly endanger lives.

choices.note: Tempting because there's a condition for ozone loss, but nothing is reversed. The argument doesn't treat 'ozone loss → nearby supernova' as if it followed from the other direction.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: A nearby supernova would strip the ozone layer; the ozone layer is thinning, so a nearby supernova must have occurred.

choices.note: Astronomers' expectation concerns our own galaxy, and nothing suggests it came from bad sources. Even if it did, it's not the core problem.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Supernovas in Andromeda happen about once a century, so they must happen once a century in our galaxy too.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Nearby' means anywhere in the galaxy in the frequency premise and within a few dozen light-years in the ozone premise. The conclusion only works if those two senses are treated as the same.

questions.stimulus: No crop variety is approved for planting by the Westfield growers' cooperative unless it is drought tolerant. Among the drought-tolerant varieties that the cooperative has field-tested, every one requires deep tilling before planting, since their roots must reach moisture far below the surface. Therefore, if a variety that the cooperative has field-tested is approved by the cooperative, that variety requires deep tilling before planting.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: No painting is displayed in the Hollis exhibit unless it has been restored. Every restored painting that the curator has examined is an oil painting. So any oil painting that the curator has examined is displayed in the Hollis exhibit.

Every member of the Arbor choir must be able to read music. Every music reader whom the director has auditioned plays the piano. So anyone the director has auditioned who plays the piano is a member of the Arbor choir.

An applicant is admitted to the translation program only if she speaks French. Each French speaker whom the director has interviewed is fluent in Spanish. Hence any applicant who has been interviewed by the director and admitted to the program is fluent in Spanish.
Every bridge in Ransom County is inspected annually. Every bridge that is inspected annually is safe for heavy trucks. So every bridge in Ransom County is safe for heavy trucks.

No vehicle is added to the city's fleet unless it passes inspection. Every vehicle that passes inspection and that the head mechanic has serviced is safe to drive. So every vehicle in the city's fleet is safe to drive.
questions.explanation: The argument's form is: all A are B; all B that are C are D; so any A that is C is D. (C) has exactly this form despite its different wording ('only if,' 'interviewed and admitted'). (E) is the most tempting trap: it has the same premises but drops the restricting condition from the conclusion, making it invalid; (D) is a valid but simpler chain with no restricting condition, and (A) and (B) reverse the inference.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Any field-tested variety that's approved requires deep tilling.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Approved → drought tolerant; drought tolerant AND field-tested → deep tilling.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are B; all B that are C are D; so any A that is C is D.

breakdown.analysis: Approved (A) → drought tolerant (B). Drought tolerant AND field-tested (C) → deep tilling (D). So approved AND field-tested → drought tolerant and field-tested → deep tilling. Valid. The key features: a restricting condition (field-tested) in the second premise, and that same restriction carried into the conclusion. Wording can change ('only if,' 'unless,' 'each'), but the logic has to line up.

choices.note: Reverses the inference. Displayed → restored; restored AND examined → oil. The conclusion says oil AND examined → displayed, which runs backward from what the premises allow.
Also backward. Member → reads music; reads music AND auditioned → piano. The conclusion goes from piano AND auditioned → member, the reverse direction.
CORRECT. Admitted → French ('only if'). French AND interviewed → Spanish. So interviewed AND admitted → Spanish. Same structure, restriction carried into the conclusion.
A valid chain, but a simpler one: all A are B, all B are D, so all A are D. There's no restricting condition like 'field-tested,' so it doesn't match.

The most tempting trap. Same premises (fleet → passed; passed AND serviced → safe) but the conclusion drops 'serviced by the head mechanic.' Without that restriction, unserviced fleet vehicles aren't covered. That's invalid; the original isn't.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: At the ancient settlement of Okrana, stone querns used for grinding grain have been found only in houses built after the settlement's defensive wall was constructed; none have been found in the many excavated houses built before the wall. Before the wall was built, therefore, Okrana's residents must have obtained grain that had already been ground elsewhere. Clearly, the wall's construction roughly coincided with the residents' beginning to process their own grain.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Querns from houses built before the wall were not removed from those houses and reused in houses built later.
Okrana's defensive wall was built in response to raids by neighboring settlements.
After the wall's construction, grain was the most important food source for Okrana's residents.
No settlement near Okrana used stone querns before Okrana's defensive wall was constructed.
The people who built the later houses at Okrana were descendants of those who built the earlier houses.
questions.explanation: The argument takes the absence of querns in earlier houses as evidence that no grinding was done there; if earlier querns had been carried off and reused in later houses, their absence would prove nothing, so (A) is required. (E) is the most tempting trap, but the argument concerns what Okrana's residents did, whoever their ancestors were; (D) is not needed and is at odds with the claim that ground grain came from elsewhere.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The wall's construction roughly coincided with Okrana residents beginning to grind their own grain.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Querns have been found only in houses built after the wall, none in the many excavated pre-wall houses; so before the wall, residents got grain already ground elsewhere.

breakdown.analysis: The argument treats 'no querns found in old houses' as 'no grinding in old houses.' That only works if the querns that would have been there didn't just get moved. Querns are tools; tools get carried around. If residents took their querns along when they moved into new houses, the old houses would look empty even though grinding happened there all along. It's like concluding nobody in your town owned a TV before 2010 because the old houses have no TVs in them now.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: querns from pre-wall houses were removed and reused in later houses. Then their absence proves nothing about pre-wall grinding, and the argument falls apart. Required.
choices.negation: Some querns from houses built before the wall were removed from those houses and reused in houses built later.

choices.note: Negate it: the wall wasn't built because of raids. Why the wall went up doesn't matter; the argument only uses it as a timeline marker. No damage.
choices.negation: Okrana's defensive wall was not built in response to raids by neighboring settlements.

choices.note: Negate it: grain wasn't the most important food after the wall. Residents could still have started grinding their own grain. No damage.
choices.negation: After the wall's construction, grain was not the most important food source for Okrana's residents.

choices.note: Not needed, and actually in tension with the argument, which says pre-wall residents got grain ground elsewhere; somebody elsewhere was grinding it. Negate it: some nearby settlement used querns earlier. That fits the argument fine.
choices.negation: At least one settlement near Okrana used stone querns before Okrana's defensive wall was constructed.

choices.note: The most tempting trap. Negate it: the later builders weren't descendants of the earlier ones. The conclusion is about when Okrana's residents started grinding grain, whoever those residents were. Still fine.
choices.negation: The people who built the later houses at Okrana were not descendants of those who built the earlier houses.

questions.stimulus: A survey of firms in the Calder region found that firms that had adopted a four-day workweek experienced, on average, no decline in output. However, nearly all of these firms adopted the four-day week voluntarily, and the firms that chose to adopt it were disproportionately ones whose managers had reported, before the change, that their employees' work could readily be compressed into fewer days. Among the few surveyed firms that adopted the four-day week because a labor contract required them to, most experienced a decline in output.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Most firms in the Calder region would experience a decline in output if they adopted a four-day workweek.
If the firms that adopted the four-day week because of a labor contract had instead adopted it voluntarily, their output would not have declined.
The four-day workweek reduces output mainly because employees work fewer total hours under it.
The survey's results do not show that a typical firm in the Calder region could adopt a four-day workweek without a decline in output.
Managers' assessments of whether their employees' work can be compressed into fewer days are generally unreliable.
questions.explanation: The firms showing no decline were self-selected for suitability, and firms required to adopt the schedule mostly saw declines, so the survey cannot be generalized to a typical firm, as (D) says. (A) is the attractive overstatement: the evidence undermines the optimistic generalization but does not show that most firms would lose output, especially given how few contract-bound firms were studied. (B) is a second trap: the evidence suggests suitability, not the voluntariness of the decision itself, explains the difference, so nothing indicates those firms would have fared better by choosing the change.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Firms that adopted a four-day week saw, on average, no output decline; 2) nearly all adopted it voluntarily; 3) adopters were disproportionately firms whose managers said beforehand their work could be compressed; 4) among the few firms forced into it by contract, most saw output decline.

breakdown.analysis: The 'no decline' result comes from a self-selected group: firms that already thought the schedule would suit them. The few firms that didn't get to choose mostly did worse. So the survey's good news can't be stretched to a typical firm. It's like surveying people who chose to run a marathon and concluding the average person can run 26 miles. But note the limit: the data doesn't prove most firms would decline either; the forced group is small.

choices.note: The attractive overstatement. The evidence undercuts the optimistic generalization, but it doesn't prove the pessimistic one. The contract-bound group was 'few,' too thin to predict what most firms would experience.
A trap. The facts point to suitability of the work as the difference, not the act of choosing. Those contract-bound firms' work may simply not compress well, so volunteering wouldn't have saved them.
Nothing about hours worked. The facts never say why output declined, so this mechanism is unsupported.

CORRECT. The no-decline firms were self-selected for suitability, and the firms without that selection mostly declined. So the survey doesn't show a typical firm could switch without losing output. Modest and well supported.
If anything, the facts suggest managers' assessments were pretty good: firms whose managers thought work could be compressed did fine. Nothing indicates the assessments are unreliable.

questions.stimulus: Hospital administrator: Our emergency department should not adopt the new triage software, even though in clinical trials it assigned treatment priority to incoming patients slightly more accurately than our nurses do. The software's developers refuse to disclose how it reaches its decisions. As a result, whenever the software made an error, our staff would have no way of determining why the error occurred or of preventing similar errors in the future.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?
choices: A medical facility should adopt any decision-making tool whose errors can be diagnosed and corrected, provided it is at least as accurate as current methods.
Developers of medical software should always disclose how their products reach decisions.
A hospital should adopt a new triage method only after it has been evaluated in clinical trials.
A medical facility should not adopt a decision-making tool whose developers will not disclose how it works, provided the facility's current method is at least as accurate as the tool.
A medical facility should not adopt a decision-making tool whose errors cannot be diagnosed unless the tool is far more accurate than the method it would replace.
questions.explanation: The software's errors cannot be diagnosed and it is only slightly more accurate than the nurses, so by (E) it should not be adopted. (D) is the most tempting trap: it targets nondisclosure, but it applies only when the current method is at least as accurate, and here the nurses are less accurate. (A) gives a condition for adopting tools whose errors can be diagnosed, which this software's cannot, and (C) is satisfied by the software's trials.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The emergency department should not adopt the new triage software.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: It's only slightly more accurate than the nurses; developers won't disclose how it decides; so staff couldn't diagnose its errors or prevent repeats.

breakdown.analysis: The principle we want says: don't adopt a tool when its errors can't be diagnosed, at least when its accuracy edge is small. The key facts to hook onto are 'errors can't be diagnosed' and 'only slightly more accurate.' A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, here 'don't adopt,' and its conditions must match the facts.

choices.note: Tells you when to adopt a tool, and only for tools whose errors can be diagnosed. This software's can't, so the principle doesn't apply, and it couldn't produce a 'don't adopt' conclusion anyway.
A rule for developers, not for the hospital. It says the developers are doing wrong, not that the hospital should reject the tool.
The software has been through clinical trials, so this condition is met. It gives no reason to reject it.

The most tempting trap. It's about nondisclosure, which is right on topic, but it only kicks in when the current method is at least as accurate as the tool. Here the nurses are slightly less accurate, so the principle doesn't apply.
CORRECT. The tool's errors can't be diagnosed, and it's only slightly (not far) more accurate than the nurses. So by this principle, don't adopt it. That's the conclusion exactly.

questions.stimulus: Musicologist: The only surviving manuscript of the anonymous Fallow Sonata contains several unusual harmonic progressions that, among all the known works of its era, appear elsewhere only in compositions by Livia Marsh. Moreover, the manuscript is written on paper bearing the watermark of a mill that supplied paper to Tarvel, the city where Marsh lived and worked. So Marsh is probably the sonata's composer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Marsh composed more sonatas than did any other composer active in Tarvel during her lifetime.
Marsh's characteristic progressions were neither published nor otherwise circulated during her lifetime, so other composers would have had little opportunity to learn them.
The mill whose watermark appears on the manuscript was the largest paper supplier in the region and sold paper in many cities.
Several of Marsh's authenticated compositions survive only in copies made by other people.
The Fallow Sonata was performed in public several times within a decade of its composition.
questions.explanation: A key gap is that another composer, perhaps one whose other works are lost, could have learned and imitated Marsh's progressions; (B) makes that much less likely. (D) is the trap: a copy made by someone else could still record a work Marsh composed, so it does not bear on authorship, while (A) is only weakly relevant and (C) weakens the watermark evidence.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Livia Marsh probably composed the Fallow Sonata.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Its unusual progressions appear, among known works, only in Marsh's compositions; the manuscript paper came from a mill that supplied Marsh's city, Tarvel.

breakdown.analysis: The progressions are the main evidence. The obvious hole: maybe someone else knew Marsh's progressions and used them, a student, an imitator, or a composer whose other works are lost. To strengthen, make it harder for anyone else to have used them. It's like identifying a forger by a secret signature trick; that only works if nobody else knew the trick.

choices.note: Marsh being prolific makes her a slightly likelier candidate in general, but it doesn't connect her to this specific sonata. Very weak.

CORRECT. If Marsh's progressions were never published or circulated, other composers had little chance to learn them. That closes the imitator gap and makes the progressions a much stronger fingerprint of Marsh.
This weakens. If the mill sold paper in many cities, the watermark no longer points specifically to Tarvel.

The trap. It might seem to explain why the manuscript isn't in her hand, but the argument never relied on handwriting. A copy by someone else could record a work by Marsh or by anyone; this doesn't bear on authorship.
Public performances don't tell us who wrote it. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Retail analyst: Any loyalty program that increases the frequency of customers' visits will raise a store's revenue, unless the program increases visit frequency mainly by attracting bargain hunters. A program increases visit frequency mainly by attracting bargain hunters only if its rewards can be redeemed solely for discounts on sale items, and a program's rewards are redeemable solely for such discounts only if the program was designed by an outside vendor. Pemberly Grocers' new loyalty program has increased the frequency of customers' visits. Hence, it will raise Pemberly's revenue.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion of the argument to be properly drawn?
choices: Any loyalty program designed by an outside vendor offers rewards that can be redeemed solely for discounts on sale items.
Most loyalty programs designed by outside vendors fail to raise a store's revenue.
Pemberly's loyalty program was not designed by an outside vendor.
Some of the customers who joined Pemberly's loyalty program are not bargain hunters.
Pemberly's loyalty program offers rewards that can be redeemed for discounts on sale items.
questions.explanation: Chaining the contrapositives: a program not designed by an outside vendor does not have sale-discount-only rewards, so it does not increase visits mainly through bargain hunters, so by the first premise it raises revenue; (C) supplies the needed fact. (A) is the trap that reverses the last conditional and so establishes nothing about Pemberly; (D) is too weak, since a program can work mainly through bargain hunters even if some members are not bargain hunters.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Pemberly's loyalty program will raise Pemberly's revenue.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Increases visits AND NOT mainly bargain hunters → raises revenue; mainly bargain hunters → sale-discount-only rewards; sale-discount-only rewards → outside vendor; Pemberly's program increased visits.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: mainly bargain hunters → discount-only rewards → outside vendor. Contrapositive: NOT outside vendor → NOT discount-only → NOT mainly bargain hunters. Pemberly's program already increases visits, so we just need 'not mainly bargain hunters,' and that's the only missing piece. The easiest way to get it is to deny the end of the chain: Pemberly's program wasn't designed by an outside vendor.

choices.note: The trap. Outside vendor → discount-only reverses the last conditional. It doesn't tell us anything about whether Pemberly's program was outside-designed or works mainly through bargain hunters.
If anything this pushes against the conclusion, and it's a 'most' statement about outside-vendor programs. It doesn't establish anything about Pemberly.
CORRECT. Not outside vendor → not discount-only → not mainly bargain hunters. Combined with increased visits, the first premise guarantees revenue goes up. Conclusion locked.
Too weak. A program can work mainly through bargain hunters even if some members aren't bargain hunters. Doesn't trigger 'not mainly bargain hunters.'
Redeemable for sale discounts (perhaps among other things) doesn't trigger any conditional. And if anything it moves toward the bargain-hunter worry, not away from it.

questions.stimulus: Epidemiologist: Long-term studies have established that, among residents of Ostrava County, walking at least five kilometers a day reduces an individual's risk of developing heart disease by 40 percent. At present, roughly one-third of the county's adult residents walk that much each day. Therefore, if every adult resident of the county who now walks less than five kilometers a day were to begin walking at least that far daily, the county's rate of heart disease among adults would fall by about 40 percent.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: infers that a change affecting only part of a population would produce, in the population as a whole, the same proportional effect that it produces in that part
takes for granted that residents who now walk little would be willing to change their habits
presumes without justification that walking is the only effective means of reducing the risk of heart disease
draws a conclusion about all regions from evidence gathered in a single county
fails to establish that heart disease is the leading cause of death among the county's residents
questions.explanation: The one-third of adults who already walk would see no further reduction, so even if everyone else cut their risk by 40 percent, the county-wide rate would fall by less than 40 percent; (A) identifies this error. (B) is the tempting trap, but the conclusion is explicitly conditional on residents changing their habits, so it does not assume they would. (D) misreads the scope: the conclusion concerns only Ostrava County.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If every adult who walks under 5 km a day started walking at least 5 km, the county's adult heart disease rate would fall by about 40%.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Walking 5+ km a day cuts an individual's heart disease risk by 40%; about one-third of adults already walk that much.

breakdown.analysis: The one-third who already walk get no new benefit. Only two-thirds of adults change. So even if each of them cuts their risk by 40%, the county-wide rate falls by less than 40%. Rough numbers: if the non-walkers account for, say, 80% of cases and those drop 40%, the total falls about 32%, not 40%. Lesson: an effect on part of a group isn't the same proportional effect on the whole group.

choices.note: CORRECT. The change only affects the two-thirds who don't already walk, yet the argument predicts the full 40% drop for the entire adult population. That's exactly the part-to-whole proportional error.
The tempting trap, but the conclusion is explicitly conditional: 'if every adult... were to begin walking.' It doesn't assume they'd actually be willing.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: A healthier diet would cut obesity in half, so obesity in our town will be cut in half next year.

choices.note: The argument doesn't need walking to be the only way to cut risk; it just predicts what walking would do.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Walking lowers heart disease risk, so anyone who doesn't walk can't lower their risk.

choices.note: The conclusion is only about Ostrava County, so there's no jump to all regions.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Walking cut heart disease 40% in Ostrava County, so it will cut it 40% everywhere.

choices.note: Whether heart disease is the leading cause of death is irrelevant to whether its rate would fall by 40%.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Walking reduces heart disease, so walking is the single most important thing for longevity here.

questions.stimulus: Most of the investigative stories that the Corbin Herald published last year relied at least partly on anonymous sources. And most of the stories published by the Herald last year that relied on anonymous sources were later publicly disputed by the people they concerned. So most of the investigative stories the Herald published last year were later publicly disputed by the people they concerned.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Most residents of Peyton commute to work by train. Everyone who commutes to work by train from Peyton buys a monthly pass. So most residents of Peyton buy a monthly pass.
