Most of the dogs at the Elmwood shelter are mixed breeds. Most of the dogs at the Elmwood shelter are under three years old. So most of the mixed-breed dogs at the Elmwood shelter are under three years old.

Some of the paintings in the Ardent Gallery's collection are by local artists. Most of the paintings by local artists in the collection were donated. So some of the paintings in the collection were donated.

Most of the tomatoes grown at the Linden farm last season were heirloom varieties. Most of the heirloom tomatoes grown at the farm last season were sold at the farmers' market. So most of the tomatoes grown at the farm last season were sold at the farmers' market.

Most employees of Tarrin Corporation work in its main office. Most employees of Tarrin Corporation have been with the company for over five years. So some employees who work in the main office have been with the company for over five years.
questions.explanation: The argument reasons: most A are B, most B are C, so most A are C, which is invalid because the two majorities need not overlap enough. (D) commits exactly this error. (B) is also flawed but in a different way, drawing a 'most' conclusion about the overlap of two groups from two 'most' statements about a single group, while (A), (C), and (E) are valid.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most of the Herald's investigative stories last year were later publicly disputed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most investigative stories used anonymous sources; most anonymous-source stories were disputed.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; most B are C; so most A are C.

breakdown.analysis: Two 'mosts' don't chain. Imagine 10 investigative stories, 6 with anonymous sources. Now say the Herald ran 100 anonymous-source stories in total, and 60 were disputed, but none of the 6 investigative ones were among them. Both premises are true; the conclusion is false. The B group can be much bigger than the A group, so the 'most B are C' majority can miss A entirely. Find the answer with the same broken chain.

choices.note: Valid, so it doesn't match a flawed argument. Most residents ride the train, and EVERY train commuter buys a pass, so those riders all buy passes: most residents buy a pass. 'All' in the second premise makes the chain work.
Flawed, but differently. It has two 'most' statements about the same group (shelter dogs) and concludes something about their overlap. The original chains A → B → C instead.
Valid. Some paintings are by local artists, and most of those were donated, so at least some paintings were donated. Nothing wrong with it.

CORRECT. Most tomatoes were heirloom; most heirloom tomatoes were sold at market; so most tomatoes were sold at market. Same most-most-most chain, same flaw: two majorities stacked on top of each other can shrink below half. Say 60 of 100 tomatoes were heirloom and 40 of those sold at market. Both premises hold, but only 40 of 100 sold.
Valid. If more than half the employees work in the main office and more than half have five-plus years, the two groups must overlap, so 'some' is guaranteed.

passages.title: Authenticating Machine-Enhanced Recordings
passages.text:
Before a court will admit a recording into evidence, the party offering it must show that the recording is what it purports to be. Traditionally, this requirement has been satisfied by a witness with personal knowledge who testifies that the recording fairly and accurately depicts the events in question. Software that enhances recordings—sharpening blurred images, filtering out noise, filling in lost frames—raises the question of how this standard should apply to altered material. Many trial courts have simply treated enhanced recordings like any others: if a witness will attest that the enhanced version accurately depicts what happened, it is admitted.

Critics of this approach, most prominently the legal scholar Mirela Vance, argue that what she calls the witness-fidelity standard fails precisely when enhancement matters most. If a witness clearly saw the detail an enhancement brings out, the enhancement adds little; but when enhancement reveals something no one observed, such as the features of a face in grainy security footage, no witness is in a position to vouch for it. Generative enhancement software does not merely clarify information already present in a recording; it predicts plausible content on the basis of patterns in the material on which it was trained. An enhanced face may thus reflect the training material as much as the person filmed. Vance proposes that courts require the proponent of an enhanced recording to disclose the software's method and to show that it has been validated on comparable material—a requirement she calls process transparency.

Defenders of the traditional approach respond that process transparency would impose heavy burdens, since many enhancement tools are proprietary and their developers resist disclosure. Cross-examination and cautionary jury instructions, they argue, are adequate to expose any weaknesses. They also point out that courts routinely admit photographs taken by cameras whose internal processing—automatic sharpening, color correction—no one in the courtroom understands.

The burden of disclosure is real, but the camera analogy is less persuasive than it first appears. Routine in-camera processing operates uniformly and modestly, and its output has been compared against reality countless times; generative enhancement, by contrast, is designed to supply detail that is absent, and its errors are by their nature plausible-looking, which makes them difficult for jurors to detect however vigorous the cross-examination. Yet Vance draws her own line in the wrong place. Not every enhancement that reveals unobserved detail invents it: software that reverses a known optical blur recovers information that, though no one saw it, the recording did capture. The relevant distinction is therefore not between what a witness observed and what no one observed, but between information a recording contains and information a program supplies. For the former, authenticating the original recording and identifying the adjustment made should suffice; the heightened showing belongs to the latter alone. Such a rule would place the burden where the risk lies without disrupting the admission of ordinary recordings.

passages.title: Overwintering Russet Dart Moths
passages.text:
Each autumn, russet dart moths in the northern part of their range fly several hundred kilometers south to overwinter, returning in spring to breed. Over the past three decades, however, entomologists surveying the Tarrow Valley have recorded growing numbers of adults that remain through the winter, entering diapause—a dormant state in which development and metabolism slow dramatically—rather than migrating. Two explanations for this change have been proposed.

The first, favored by ecologist Ilse Marrow and her colleagues, holds that the change is a direct response to milder winters. On this view, every russet dart possesses the capacity to enter diapause, and whether a given moth migrates or stays depends on the temperature cues it experiences as it matures. Warmer autumns would therefore tip more individuals toward diapause, and warmer winters would allow more of them to survive until spring. In support of this hypothesis, Marrow's group has shown that the proportion of resident moths in a given year correlates closely with that year's autumn temperatures. Marrow concedes that the correlation is imperfect, but she attributes the remaining variation to differences in winter severity, which affect survival only after the decision to stay has been made.

A second hypothesis, advanced by Dariusz Pell, holds that the shift reflects heritable change. Migration is costly and dangerous; if Tarrow winters have become survivable, moths with an inherited predisposition to remain would leave more offspring than those inclined to migrate, and the predisposition would spread. To test this, Pell's group collected eggs from Tarrow residents and from migrants and reared the larvae under identical temperature and day-length conditions. Offspring of residents proved far more likely to enter diapause than offspring of migrants. Because the rearing environment was held constant, Pell argues, the difference must reflect inheritance. As Pell acknowledges, however, his selective argument presupposes that residents now survive Tarrow winters at least as well as migrants survive the journey south—a comparison no one has yet measured directly.

The two hypotheses are not mutually exclusive. Marrow's correlation shows that temperature matters in any given year, but not that temperature is the only factor; Pell's experiment reveals a heritable component but leaves open whether temperature modulates its expression. A plausible synthesis is that warming has acted in two ways at once: immediately, by tipping marginal individuals toward diapause, and over generations, by favoring moths inclined to stay. This synthesis yields a testable prediction. If heritable change has occurred, then a given autumn temperature should now send a higher proportion of moths into diapause than it did thirty years ago. A preliminary reanalysis of the valley's autumn survey records suggests that it does, although the records from the earliest years are too sparse to settle the matter.

passages.title: Irregularity in Kestel Strip Weaving
passages.text:
For much of the twentieth century, collectors who prized the strip-woven cloths of the Kestel highlands described them in terms that emphasized spontaneity. These cloths are made of narrow bands woven separately and then sewn together edge to edge, and the bands rarely align: a stripe in one band stops short of its counterpart in the next, and motifs that might be expected to form a continuous line across the cloth instead jump and stagger. Dealers' catalogues attributed these misalignments to the weavers' indifference to precision, praising the cloths as artless expressions of a culture untouched by the discipline of the workshop.

This account has been challenged by textile historians, who point out that Kestel weavers were capable of exact alignment when they chose. Cloths made for funerals, which survive in smaller numbers, are almost perfectly matched across their seams. Moreover, the instructions recorded from the last generation of practicing weavers include specific terms for different kinds of offset—one for a stagger of half a motif, another for a full reversal of a motif's direction—suggesting that offsets were planned and named, not merely tolerated.

Recognizing that the misalignments were deliberate, however, is only a first step; it does not tell us what they meant. Some historians have proposed that each type of offset carried a fixed symbolic meaning, much as a word does. The evidence for this is thin. The weavers' terms for offsets describe their visual form rather than anything they might stand for, and the same offset appears on cloths made for very different occasions. To be sure, this does not rule the view out: the recorded instructions were gathered to teach technique, and meanings reserved for ritual settings may never have been spoken to outsiders. A more plausible view is that the offsets functioned less like a vocabulary than like rhythm in music: what mattered was not what any single offset signified but the pattern of expectation and variation that the offsets created across the whole cloth. On this view, the near-perfect alignment of funeral cloths is significant precisely as an absence of rhythm—a stillness suited to mourning.

The collectors' error, then, was not simply a factual one. By treating irregularity as a lack of control, they assumed that the proper standard for judging cloth was the uniformity achieved by the industrial loom, and that the Kestel weavers had fallen short of it. Their praise for the cloths' artlessness was thus a backhanded compliment, admiring the weavers for a failure they had not committed. The weavers were working toward a different standard entirely, one in which variation was the very medium of the art rather than evidence of an inability to master it.

passages.title: Mixed-Income Housing and Social Networks
passages.text:
Passage A

Mixed-income housing has been promoted on the theory that when households of different incomes live side by side, lower-income residents will gain access to social networks that carry information about jobs and other opportunities. The evidence for this mechanism is discouraging. In a five-year study of the Linden Court development, sociologist Tomas Arquero found that residents formed friendships overwhelmingly within their own income group; conversations across groups were mostly brief and concerned practical matters such as parking and noise. Advocates reply that five years is too short a time for trust to develop across lines of class. Arquero grants the point in principle, but notes that the few cross-group friendships he did observe had all formed within the first year, and that none formed thereafter. Similar patterns have been reported elsewhere. Residents of different incomes also tend to use different spaces: higher-income tenants often drive to stores outside the neighborhood and enroll their children in private schools, while lower-income tenants rely on neighborhood shops, schools, and clinics.

Proximity alone, it seems, does not produce the ties that the policy's advocates anticipated. People form relationships through repeated, purposeful contact, and sharing an address provides little of that. If the goal is to widen the networks of low-income households, resources might be better directed toward programs that create such contact directly—mentoring programs, job-placement partnerships, cooperative workplaces—than toward costly construction projects whose social benefits rest on an unrealistic picture of how neighbors interact.

Passage B

Critics of mixed-income housing often measure its success by counting friendships across income lines, and by that measure it frequently disappoints. But this standard misconstrues how residential settings shape opportunity. Much of what neighbors provide one another flows not through close relationships but through weak ties: a passing remark that a hospital is hiring, a familiar face who can vouch for a job applicant. Such exchanges are easily missed by surveys that ask residents to name their friends.

More important, the influence of a mixed neighborhood operates largely through institutions rather than through individual relationships. Higher-income households tend to press local officials, often successfully, for well-maintained parks, safer streets, and more responsive public services, and lower-income residents share in these improvements whether or not they ever speak to their wealthier neighbors. Researchers studying the Harrow Street redevelopment found that the arrival of higher-income tenants was followed within three years by expanded bus service and a renovated public library—improvements that longtime residents had requested for a decade without success. None of this shows that mixed-income housing is the most efficient way to secure such improvements; a city could in principle provide them directly. In practice, however, officials respond most readily to residents who vote, organize, and complain effectively, and mixing incomes changes who is doing the asking. Gains of this kind are real, even though they would never appear in a tally of cross-class friendships, and any fair assessment of mixed-income housing must take them into account.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Because no witness can vouch for details that no one observed, courts should require a heightened showing of reliability for any enhancement that reveals such details, whatever its method.

Courts should require a heightened showing of reliability for enhancements that supply information a recording does not contain, but not for enhancements that recover or adjust information the recording captured.
The traditional authentication standard remains adequate for enhanced recordings, because cross-examination and jury instructions can expose any weaknesses in an enhancement.
Generative enhancement software is so prone to plausible-looking errors that recordings enhanced by it should be excluded from evidence altogether.
Courts that routinely admit photographs from cameras with automatic internal processing have no principled basis for treating enhanced recordings any differently.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph states the author's thesis: the line falls between information a recording contains and information a program supplies, with the heightened showing reserved for the latter, which is B. A is the trap: it is Vance's line (observed versus unobserved), which the author says is 'drawn in the wrong place,' since deblurring can reveal unobserved but captured detail. C and E are the defenders' positions, which the author rejects, and D overstates a showing requirement as exclusion.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall point: what rule the author wants courts to use for enhanced recordings.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, especially "The relevant distinction is therefore..." and the sentence after it. Paragraphs 2-3 are views the author is reacting to.

breakdown.analysis: This passage has three voices: the courts (P1), Vance (P2), the defenders (P3). The author only speaks up in P4, and that's where the main point lives. The author says Vance is right about the risk but drew the line in the wrong place: the line isn't observed vs. unobserved, it's contained vs. supplied. Prephrase: heightened showing only for enhancements that add information the recording never had. Lesson: in a multi-viewpoint passage, the main point is the author's view, not the first critic's.

choices.note: This is Vance's rule, not the author's. It draws the line at "details no one observed," and the author says that line is in the wrong place, because deblurring can reveal unobserved detail the recording really captured. It's the trap because it sounds like the critical position the author partly agrees with.

CORRECT. This is the P4 thesis in plain words: heightened showing for information the program supplies, ordinary showing for information the recording contains. It also captures the "but not" half, which is what separates the author from Vance.
This is the defenders' view from P3. The author rejects it: generative errors are plausible-looking and hard to catch "however vigorous the cross-examination." Opposite of the author.
Too strong. The author never says exclude these recordings. The author says they need a heightened showing. A higher bar to get in is not a ban.

This is the defenders' camera analogy, which the author spends P4 knocking down. The author thinks there IS a principled basis: in-camera processing is modest and tested; generative enhancement invents detail.

questions.stem: According to the passage, generative enhancement software differs from tools that merely clarify a recording in that generative software
choices: is used primarily on security footage rather than on audio recordings
cannot be applied to recordings that have lost frames because of a faulty connection
has been compared against reality more often than in-camera processing has
is typically developed by companies that are willing to disclose their methods
predicts plausible content on the basis of patterns in the material on which it was trained
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says generative software 'does not merely clarify information already present' but 'predicts plausible content on the basis of patterns in the material on which it was trained,' which is E. C is the trap: it uses the passage's own phrase but reverses the comparison, since it is in-camera processing whose output 'has been compared against reality countless times.' D contradicts the defenders' point that developers resist disclosure.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says makes generative enhancement different from tools that just clarify.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, the sentence starting "Generative enhancement software does not merely clarify..."

breakdown.analysis: Detail question, so the answer is sitting in a sentence. P2 says generative software "does not merely clarify information already present"; it "predicts plausible content" based on its training material. Prephrase: it guesses/fills in based on training data. Lesson: on a detail question, go back and find the line. Don't answer from memory.

choices.note: Not in the passage. Security footage is just an example of where enhancement matters; nothing says generative tools are mainly used there, and audio is never contrasted.
Made up. Filling in lost frames is listed as something enhancement software does. Nothing says generative software can't handle lost frames.
Reversed. It's in-camera processing whose output "has been compared against reality countless times." This is a trap that borrows the passage's own words and flips who they describe.
Opposite. The defenders say many tools are proprietary and developers resist disclosure.

CORRECT. Near-verbatim from P2: generative software "predicts plausible content on the basis of patterns in the material on which it was trained." That's exactly what separates it from clarifying what's already there.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would regard which one of the following as sufficient for admitting a recording enhanced by software that reverses a known optical blur, making legible a license plate that no witness was able to read?
choices: authentication of the original recording together with identification of the adjustment that was made
disclosure of the software's method together with evidence that it has been validated on comparable material
testimony by a witness with personal knowledge that the enhanced recording accurately depicts the license plate
a cautionary jury instruction explaining that the enhancement may contain plausible-looking errors
a showing that the software was not trained on images of license plates resembling the one depicted
questions.explanation: The author classifies reversing a known blur as recovering 'information that, though no one saw it, the recording did capture,' and says that for such information 'authenticating the original recording and identifying the adjustment made should suffice,' which is A. B is the trap: it is the heightened showing Vance would demand because the detail was unobserved, but the author reserves it for supplied information. C is impossible on the facts, since no witness could read the plate.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author's rule to a case: blur-reversal software makes a license plate readable that no witness could read. What would the author say is enough to admit it?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: the optical-blur example and the sentence "For the former, authenticating the original recording and identifying the adjustment made should suffice."

breakdown.analysis: The author uses this exact example. Reversing a known blur recovers information the recording captured, even though nobody saw it. So it falls in the "contained" bucket. For that bucket the author says: authenticate the original and identify the adjustment. Done. Prephrase: the ordinary, lighter showing. Lesson: on an application question, first sort the case into the author's categories, then read off the rule for that category.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the author's "should suffice" standard for information the recording contains, and the blur example is the author's own illustration of that category.

This is the heightened showing (Vance's process transparency). Vance would demand it because no one saw the plate. But the author reserves it for supplied information, and blur reversal isn't that. Classic trap: right rule, wrong bucket.
Impossible on the facts: no witness could read the plate, so no witness can vouch that the enhanced plate is accurate. That's the whole problem with the witness standard.

Jury instructions are the defenders' remedy, and the author thinks they don't work for generative errors. Also, the question asks what's sufficient for admission, and the author named a specific showing; this isn't it.
Training data matters for generative software, which supplies detail. Blur reversal doesn't predict from training material, so this showing is beside the point. The author never mentions it.

questions.stem: The author mentions that the output of routine in-camera processing 'has been compared against reality countless times' primarily in order to
choices: concede that the traditional approach has a sound basis in the case of ordinary photographs
suggest that generative enhancement software will eventually become as reliable as in-camera processing
explain why defenders of the traditional approach regard process transparency as unduly burdensome
show that jurors already understand how cameras alter the images they record
identify a difference that weakens an analogy offered by defenders of the traditional approach
questions.explanation: The remark follows the claim that 'the camera analogy is less persuasive than it first appears' and contrasts tested, modest in-camera processing with generative enhancement, which is E. A is tempting because the remark does imply that ordinary photographs are reliable, but its role is to distinguish the two cases, not to concede ground to the defenders. D contradicts the defenders' premise that no one in the courtroom understands in-camera processing.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author says in-camera processing "has been compared against reality countless times."

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first two sentences; the camera analogy it responds to is at the end of paragraph 3.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence before: "the camera analogy is less persuasive than it first appears." Then the author lists ways camera processing differs from generative enhancement: uniform, modest, tested. So the phrase is a point of difference used to break the defenders' analogy. Prephrase: to show cameras and generative tools aren't alike. Lesson: function questions are about why it's there, so read the sentence right before it.

choices.note: Tempting, since the line does imply ordinary photos are reliable. But the point isn't to give the defenders ground; it's to separate cameras from generative enhancement. Right implication, wrong purpose.
No prediction about the future appears. The author contrasts them as they are now: generative enhancement is "designed to supply detail that is absent."
Wrong topic. The burden argument is about proprietary tools and disclosure. The "compared against reality" line answers the camera analogy, a separate defender point.
Contradicts the passage. The defenders' premise is that no one in the courtroom understands in-camera processing. The author's point is about testing, not juror understanding.

CORRECT. The defenders say: we admit camera photos without understanding the processing, so why not enhanced recordings? The author answers with a difference: camera processing is modest and tested, generative enhancement isn't. That weakens the analogy.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Vance's proposal of process transparency is best described as
choices: unreserved support for requiring it of every party that offers an enhanced recording in evidence
sympathy for its aims, tempered by the judgment that the disclosure burden it imposes can never be justified
agreement with the concern behind it, combined with the view that a different criterion should determine when it applies
agreement that it should be required only for recordings whose enhanced details no witness observed
rejection of it in favor of reliance on cross-examination and cautionary jury instructions
questions.explanation: The author rebuts the camera analogy, accepting Vance's worry about plausible-looking generative errors, but says she 'draws her own line in the wrong place' and substitutes the contained/supplied distinction, which is C. D is the most tempting trap: it describes Vance's own observed/unobserved line, the very criterion the author rejects. B misreads the concession that 'the burden of disclosure is real'; the author thinks the burden is justified where the risk lies.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the author feels about Vance's process-transparency proposal.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: the rebuttal of the camera analogy (agreeing with Vance's worry) and "Yet Vance draws her own line in the wrong place."

breakdown.analysis: Mixed attitude. The author sides with Vance against the defenders: generative errors are real and hard to catch. But then: "Yet Vance draws her own line in the wrong place." The author keeps the heightened showing but changes when it kicks in (supplied info, not unobserved info). Prephrase: agrees with the worry, disagrees about the trigger. Lesson: when the author says "yet" after defending someone, the answer is almost always "yes, but."

choices.note: Too strong. "Unreserved" and "every party" ignore the author's main move: limit the requirement to supplied information, not every enhanced recording.

Half right, then wrong. The author concedes "the burden of disclosure is real," but never says it can't be justified. The author's rule places the burden "where the risk lies," so it is justified there.

CORRECT. Agreement with the concern (plausible-looking generative errors, weak witness vouching) plus a different criterion for when the requirement applies (contained vs. supplied instead of observed vs. unobserved).

The big trap. "Only for recordings whose enhanced details no witness observed" is Vance's own line, the one the author says is in the wrong place. Under that line the license-plate deblur would need the heightened showing; the author says it wouldn't.
That's the defenders. The author explicitly says cross-examination can't reliably catch plausible-looking errors.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, Vance would most likely hold that an enhanced recording's potential value as evidence and the ability of a witness to authenticate the enhanced version tend to be
choices: inversely related, since the more an enhancement reveals, the more likely it is that the software used was generative
unrelated, since authentication concerns only whether the recording has been altered
inversely related, since the details a witness can vouch for are those that the enhancement least needs to supply
inversely related, since witnesses tend to overstate the accuracy of recordings that corroborate their own accounts
directly related, since jurors give greater weight to recordings that a witness has authenticated
questions.explanation: Vance argues that if a witness clearly saw a detail, enhancement 'adds little,' while when enhancement reveals what no one observed, no witness can vouch for it; so value and authenticability vary inversely for exactly the reason in C. A is the strongest trap: it gets the relationship right but grounds it in the generative/non-generative distinction, which Vance raises as a separate, compounding problem, not as the basis of her witness argument (and the passage never says revealing more makes generative software likelier). D likewise has the right relation but an invented reason, witness bias.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Figure out how Vance would relate two things: how valuable an enhanced recording is, and whether a witness can vouch for it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, the second sentence: "If a witness clearly saw the detail ... the enhancement adds little; but when enhancement reveals something no one observed ... no witness is in a position to vouch for it."

breakdown.analysis: Vance's point: the standard "fails precisely when enhancement matters most." If the witness saw it, enhancement adds little (low value, easy to vouch). If no one saw it, enhancement matters a lot (high value, no one can vouch). So they move in opposite directions, and the reason is that what a witness can confirm is what the enhancement didn't need to add. Prephrase: inversely related, because witnesses can only vouch for what they already saw. Lesson: three answers say "inversely related" here, so the reason is what you're really choosing between.

choices.note: Right relationship, wrong reason. Vance's witness argument doesn't depend on generative vs. non-generative software; that's a separate problem she raises next. And the passage never says revealing more makes generative software more likely.
Wrong relationship, and it misdescribes authentication. Authentication is about whether the recording accurately depicts events, not just whether it was altered. Vance clearly sees a link.
CORRECT. This is Vance's reasoning: details a witness can vouch for are ones they saw, and those are exactly the details enhancement adds little to. Value up, vouchability down.
Right relationship, invented reason. Witness bias toward recordings that support their story appears nowhere in the passage.
Wrong direction. Vance's whole point is that the standard fails when enhancement matters most, which is an inverse relationship. Juror weighting isn't discussed.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the rule the author proposes in the last paragraph?
choices: A museum lets conservators remove discolored varnish to expose original pigments, even colors no living viewer has seen, with an ordinary treatment record, but requires repainting of lost areas to be justified by verified comparable works.

A museum requires special justification from verified comparable works for any treatment that exposes features of a painting that no living viewer has ever seen, but permits routine surface cleaning on the basis of an ordinary treatment record.
A museum forbids conservators to repaint lost areas of any painting under any circumstances, while allowing them to clean and revarnish paintings on the basis of an ordinary treatment record.
A museum requires conservators to justify every treatment of every painting, however minor, by reference to verified comparable works before the painting may be displayed.
A museum requires justification from verified comparable works only for restorations performed by outside contractors, whose methods its own staff cannot directly supervise.
questions.explanation: The author's rule turns on whether information was contained in the original (ordinary showing, even if no one observed it) or supplied by the process (heightened showing); exposing pigments that are there versus repainting what is lost maps onto this, which is A. B is the trap: it draws the line by what no one has seen, which is Vance's criterion that the author rejects. C corresponds to excluding generated content rather than admitting it on a heightened showing, and D applies the heightened showing across the board.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the situation that follows the same rule as the author's proposal.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, last three sentences: the contained/supplied distinction and which showing goes with each.

breakdown.analysis: Strip the author's rule down: if the process recovers what's really there (even if nobody has seen it), use the ordinary showing; if the process adds what isn't there, require the heightened showing. Prephrase for a museum: uncovering original paint = ordinary record, even if no one alive has seen it; filling in lost paint = strong justification. Lesson: on analogy questions, match the dividing line, not the subject matter. The wrong answers here mostly draw a different line.

choices.note: CORRECT. Removing varnish exposes pigments that are actually there (contained), even ones no viewer has seen, so an ordinary record suffices. Repainting lost areas supplies what's gone, so it needs verified comparables (heightened showing). Same line, same two outcomes.
The trap. It draws the line at "features no living viewer has ever seen," which is Vance's observed/unobserved line. The author would put uncovering unseen original paint in the ordinary category.
Forbidding repainting outright matches excluding generated content. The author doesn't exclude it; the author admits it on a heightened showing. Too strong.
No distinction at all: every treatment gets the heavy showing. The author's rule specifically spares the contained category from that burden.
Wrong line. This divides by who does the work (outside contractors vs. staff), not by whether the treatment recovers or supplies content.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The increase in overwintering russet darts in the Tarrow Valley is best explained as a direct response to milder autumns and winters.
Pell's rearing experiment demonstrates that the tendency of russet darts to overwinter is inherited rather than environmentally determined.
Migration has become more costly for russet darts than overwintering, because warming has made the journey south more dangerous.
The rise in overwintering russet darts has probably resulted from both an immediate response to temperature and heritable change, a view that preliminary evidence tends to support.
The rise in overwintering russet darts has resulted from both an immediate response to temperature and heritable change, as a reanalysis of survey records has now confirmed.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph calls the synthesis 'plausible' and says preliminary reanalysis 'suggests' its prediction holds, although early records are 'too sparse to settle the matter,' which matches the hedged claim in D. E is the trap: same content, but 'has now confirmed' overstates the author's commitment. A and B each state only one of the hypotheses the author combines.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall point about why more russet darts are staying through winter.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: "A plausible synthesis..." and the last sentence about preliminary evidence.

breakdown.analysis: P2 is Marrow (temperature), P3 is Pell (heredity), P4 is the author: both are probably at work, and early evidence leans that way but isn't conclusive. Notice the hedges: "plausible," "suggests," "too sparse to settle the matter." Prephrase: probably both causes, tentatively supported. Lesson: match the author's confidence level, not just the content. Two answers here say the same thing with different certainty.

choices.note: That's only Marrow's hypothesis. The author says temperature isn't shown to be the only factor and adds a heritable component.

Only Pell's side, and overstated. The author says Pell's experiment reveals a heritable component but "leaves open" whether temperature also matters. "Rather than environmentally determined" is an either/or the author rejects.
Distorts Pell's premise. The passage says Tarrow winters have become survivable, not that the journey south has become more dangerous. And this isn't the main point anyway.
CORRECT. Both causes, "probably," and evidence that "tends to support." That matches "plausible synthesis" and a reanalysis that "suggests" but can't settle it.
The trap. Same content as D, but "has now confirmed" is too strong. The author says the early records are "too sparse to settle the matter." Watch the switch from suggests to confirms.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Pell's group concluded that the tendency to overwinter has a heritable component because
choices: the proportion of resident moths in the Tarrow Valley has risen steadily over three decades
offspring of resident and migrant moths reared under identical conditions differed in their tendency to enter diapause
resident moths have been shown to survive Tarrow winters at least as well as migrants survive the journey south
the proportion of resident moths in a given year correlates closely with that year's autumn temperatures
larvae reared at warmer temperatures were more likely to enter diapause than larvae reared at cooler temperatures
questions.explanation: The third paragraph reports that larvae from residents and migrants reared under identical conditions differed, with residents' offspring far more likely to enter diapause, which is B. C is the trap: the passage says Pell's argument presupposes this survival comparison but that 'no one has yet measured' it. D is Marrow's evidence, and E describes a temperature effect that Pell's design held constant.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the evidence Pell used to conclude the overwintering tendency is inherited.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, the rearing experiment and "Because the rearing environment was held constant..."

breakdown.analysis: Pell raised eggs from residents and migrants under the same conditions. Residents' offspring entered diapause far more often. Same environment, different outcome, so (he argues) the difference must be inherited. Prephrase: the identical-conditions rearing result. Lesson: keep each scientist's evidence in its own box; RC detail questions love swapping them.

choices.note: That's the phenomenon both hypotheses try to explain, not Pell's evidence for heritability. A rising count can't tell you why it's rising.
CORRECT. This is the experiment: identical temperature and day length, yet residents' offspring entered diapause far more often. That's Pell's basis for inheritance.
The trap. This is something Pell's selective argument presupposes, and the passage says "no one has yet measured" it. It can't be what his conclusion rests on as shown evidence.
That's Marrow's evidence (P2), not Pell's.
Pell held temperature constant, so his experiment couldn't show a temperature effect. This describes a design he didn't use.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that if Marrow's hypothesis were the complete explanation for the rise in overwintering moths, then offspring of Tarrow residents and offspring of migrants reared under identical conditions would be expected to
choices: enter diapause at a higher rate than either group's parents did
migrate in larger numbers than their parents did
fail to enter diapause unless reared under the day-length conditions of the Tarrow Valley
differ in their tendency to enter diapause only if reared at low temperatures
enter diapause at roughly equal rates
questions.explanation: On Marrow's view every moth has the same capacity for diapause and the decision depends on the temperature cues experienced during maturation; if that were the whole story, offspring given identical cues should behave alike, which is E. D is the trap: temperature is central to Marrow's view, but nothing in her hypothesis gives the two groups different responses at any temperature. A introduces a comparison with the parents that the hypothesis does not address.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict what Pell's experiment would have shown if Marrow's hypothesis were the whole story.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2: "every russet dart possesses the capacity to enter diapause, and whether a given moth migrates or stays depends on the temperature cues it experiences." Paragraph 3 for the experiment.

breakdown.analysis: Marrow's view: all moths are the same underneath; only the temperature they experience decides. Pell's experiment gave both groups the same conditions. If Marrow is completely right, same cues → same behavior. Prephrase: the two groups would enter diapause at about the same rate. Think of identical twins raised in the same house: if only environment matters, they turn out the same.

choices.note: Brings in the parents, which Marrow's hypothesis doesn't address. The lab conditions could be warmer or colder than what the parents saw; nothing predicts a rise.
Nothing in Marrow's view predicts more migration. And the question is about the two groups compared with each other, not with their parents.
Marrow's view is about temperature cues, and nothing says Tarrow day length is required for diapause. Invented condition.

The trap. Temperature is central to Marrow, but her hypothesis gives every moth the same capacity, so there's no reason the two groups would respond differently at low temperatures or any other temperature.

CORRECT. If every moth has the same capacity and only the cues decide, identical cues should yield roughly equal rates. Pell's actual result (a big difference) is what shows Marrow isn't the whole story.

questions.stem: The author's statement that Marrow's correlation 'shows that temperature matters in any given year, but not that temperature is the only factor' serves primarily to
choices: indicate that the evidence offered for one hypothesis does not exclude the other
suggest that Marrow's correlation is too imperfect to support her hypothesis
concede that Pell's experiment fails to establish a heritable component
explain why Marrow attributes the remaining variation to differences in winter severity
establish that temperature influences the expression of the heritable trait Pell identified
questions.explanation: The sentence opens the author's case that the hypotheses 'are not mutually exclusive': Marrow's correlation is compatible with an additional heritable factor, which is A. B is a strong trap because the passage does report that the correlation is imperfect, but the author's point concerns what the correlation fails to rule out, not its weakness. E is the other trap: the author says Pell's experiment 'leaves open whether temperature modulates' the trait's expression, so asserting that it does overstates the author's commitment.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author says Marrow's correlation shows temperature matters "but not that temperature is the only factor."

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first two sentences: "The two hypotheses are not mutually exclusive" and what follows.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence right before is the claim: the hypotheses aren't mutually exclusive. This line supports that by showing Marrow's evidence leaves room for Pell's factor (and the second half shows Pell's leaves room for temperature). Prephrase: to show Marrow's evidence doesn't rule out the heritable explanation. Lesson: a function answer should tie the line to the claim it supports.

choices.note: CORRECT. The author is showing that Marrow's evidence is compatible with an additional heritable factor, which is the first step in arguing the two hypotheses can both be true.

Tempting, because P2 does say the correlation is imperfect. But the author doesn't call it too weak; the author says it "shows that temperature matters." The point is what it fails to exclude, not that it's flimsy.
Wrong hypothesis and wrong claim. This line is about Marrow's correlation, and the author says Pell's experiment does reveal a heritable component.
That's Marrow's own explanation from P2 for the leftover variation. The author's sentence isn't explaining Marrow's move; it's assessing her evidence.
Too strong. The author says Pell's experiment "leaves open whether temperature modulates" the trait's expression. Leaving it open isn't establishing it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken Pell's argument that the results of the rearing experiment must reflect inheritance?
choices: Resident moths survive Tarrow winters at substantially lower rates than migrant moths survive the long journey south to their wintering grounds.
Some offspring of migrant moths in Pell's experiment entered diapause, though at a much lower rate than offspring of residents.
Female russet darts deposit hormones in their eggs that reflect the temperatures the females themselves experienced, and these hormones influence whether the larvae later enter diapause.
In the wild, the offspring of resident moths are exposed to colder temperatures during larval development than are the offspring of migrant moths.
Larvae of both groups in Pell's laboratory entered diapause at lower rates than larvae of either group do in the wild.
questions.explanation: Pell infers inheritance because the rearing environment was identical; if mothers pass an environmentally induced signal through the egg, the offspring differed before rearing began for a non-genetic reason, which is C. A is the most tempting trap: it undermines Pell's selective account of why a predisposition would spread, which the passage says he presupposes, but it does nothing to the separate inference from the experiment that a heritable difference exists. D concerns wild conditions the experiment eliminated, and E affects both groups equally, leaving the difference intact.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undercuts Pell's inference that the experiment's results must be due to inheritance.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3: "Because the rearing environment was held constant, Pell argues, the difference must reflect inheritance."

breakdown.analysis: Pell's logic: same rearing environment + different outcome → inheritance. The gap: something besides genes could differ between the groups before rearing starts. If something non-genetic is passed from mother to egg, the "identical environment" didn't really start from identical. Prephrase: a non-genetic difference carried in from the parents. It's like saying two kids raised in the same school score differently, so it must be genetic, ignoring that one had a tutor at home before school.

choices.note: The most tempting trap. This hurts Pell's separate selective story (why a stay-at-home trait would spread). It does nothing to the experiment's inference that a heritable difference exists. The question targets the experiment.
No problem for Pell. His result is a difference in rates, not all-or-nothing. Some migrants' offspring entering diapause at a much lower rate fits fine.

CORRECT. Mothers' eggs carry hormones reflecting the temperatures the mothers felt, and those hormones affect diapause. Residents' mothers wintered in Tarrow; migrants' mothers didn't. So the offspring differed for an environmental, non-genetic reason before rearing began. That breaks "held constant, so it must be inheritance."
About wild conditions. Pell's experiment removed those differences by rearing both groups the same way, so this doesn't touch his result.
Affects both groups equally. Lab rates being lower overall leaves the difference between groups intact, and the difference is what Pell relies on.

questions.stem: The author's proposed test suggests which one of the following?
choices: If heritable change has occurred, the correlation between autumn temperature and the proportion of moths entering diapause should have weakened over the decades.
If autumn temperature cues alone determined whether moths enter diapause, the proportion entering diapause at a given autumn temperature would have remained roughly stable over the decades.
If Marrow's hypothesis is correct, the number of migrants returning to the Tarrow Valley each spring should have declined over the decades.
If the synthesis is correct, every recent year should show a higher proportion of moths entering diapause than any year thirty years ago, regardless of autumn temperatures.
If both hypotheses are correct, a cold autumn should now send a lower proportion of moths into diapause than a cold autumn did thirty years ago.
questions.explanation: The test treats a rise, at a fixed autumn temperature, in the proportion entering diapause as the signature of heritable change; the implied contrast is that if temperature cues alone governed the decision, that proportion would hold roughly steady across decades, which is B. A is a strong trap: an upward shift at every temperature is compatible with an unchanged correlation, so the test implies nothing about the correlation weakening. D overstates the synthesis, which keeps a year-to-year temperature effect, and E reverses the predicted direction.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the author's proposed test implies.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: "If heritable change has occurred, then a given autumn temperature should now send a higher proportion of moths into diapause than it did thirty years ago."

breakdown.analysis: The test: hold temperature fixed and compare across decades. Heritable change → higher proportion now at the same temperature. The flip side is what makes it a test: if temperature cues alone decided, the same temperature should produce about the same proportion then and now. Prephrase: under a temperature-only story, the rate at a given temperature stays flat over time. Lesson: a test only works if the rival view predicts something different; finding that rival prediction is the inference.

choices.note: The trap. Heritable change shifts the whole curve up: more diapause at every temperature. The correlation can stay just as strong after a shift like that. The test says nothing about it weakening.

CORRECT. If only temperature cues matter, a given temperature should produce roughly the same proportion in any decade. That's the baseline the author's test is comparing against; a rise means something else (heredity) is going on.
The test is about proportions entering diapause at a given temperature, not counts of migrants returning in spring. The passage doesn't link Marrow's view to that number.

Overstates the synthesis. It keeps a year-to-year temperature effect, so a very cold recent year could still have a lower proportion than a warm year long ago. "Regardless of autumn temperatures" ignores half the synthesis.
Reversed. Heritable change predicts a higher proportion at a given temperature, including a cold one, not a lower proportion.

questions.stem: Which one of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A theory is described, an anomaly that the theory cannot accommodate is identified, and a replacement theory is proposed.
A change is described, two explanations and the evidence for each are presented, and the author argues that the explanations can be combined and proposes a way to test the combination.
Two explanations of a phenomenon are presented, one is shown to rest on flawed evidence, and the other is endorsed with qualifications and a proposal for further study.
A phenomenon is described, an experiment designed to explain it is criticized in detail, and further research using a larger set of survey records is recommended.
A hypothesis is stated, evidence for it is presented, and objections to it are raised and answered in turn.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the rise in overwintering moths, presents Marrow's and Pell's explanations with their evidence and limitations, then argues for a synthesis with a testable prediction, which is B. C is the trap: the passage notes limitations of both explanations (an imperfect correlation, an unmeasured survival comparison) but rejects neither, saying each shows something real. A and E misdescribe the passage as centered on a single theory.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the passage is organized, paragraph by paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: All four paragraphs: P1 change, P2 Marrow, P3 Pell, P4 synthesis and test.

breakdown.analysis: Quick map. P1: moths are staying instead of migrating; two explanations exist. P2: Marrow's temperature explanation and evidence. P3: Pell's heritable explanation and evidence. P4: they're compatible; here's a combined view and a test. Prephrase: change, two explanations with evidence, combine them, test it. Lesson: check every piece of the answer against your map; one wrong verb ("rejected," "criticized") kills it.

choices.note: Nothing is replaced. The author keeps both explanations and combines them. And the passage opens with a phenomenon, not a single theory.
CORRECT. Every piece matches: the change (P1), two explanations with evidence (P2-P3), the argument that they're compatible plus a synthesis (P4), and the testable prediction (P4).
The trap. The passage notes limits on both (imperfect correlation, unmeasured survival comparison), but neither is shown to rest on flawed evidence. The author endorses a combination, not one side.
Pell's experiment isn't "criticized in detail"; it's credited with revealing a heritable component. And the survey records are a reanalysis already underway, not a recommendation for a larger set.
Misses that there are two hypotheses treated evenly. There's no single hypothesis defended against objections.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that the misalignments in Kestel cloths were deliberate rather than the result of the weavers' indifference to precision
argue that funeral cloths are the most artistically accomplished works of the Kestel weaving tradition
explain the technical process by which Kestel cloths are woven in bands and assembled
defend an interpretation of the misalignments in Kestel cloths that rejects one earlier account and refines another
show that the misalignments in Kestel cloths constitute a symbolic vocabulary whose meanings can be recovered
questions.explanation: The author rejects the collectors' account, accepts the historians' finding that misalignments were deliberate, and then goes further by arguing against the fixed-symbol view and for a rhythmic one, which is D. A is the trap: deliberateness is only what the author calls 'a first step,' so A captures one paragraph's point rather than the passage's purpose. E states the vocabulary view the author doubts.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage as a whole is trying to do.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The pivots: paragraph 2 (historians reject the collectors), paragraph 3 ("only a first step" and "A more plausible view"), paragraph 4 (the collectors' deeper error).

breakdown.analysis: Three layers. Collectors: misalignments are sloppiness. Historians: no, they're deliberate. Author: right, but that's only a first step; the meaning isn't a vocabulary, it's rhythm. So the author throws out one account (collectors) and builds on another (historians' deliberateness). Prephrase: argue for a rhythm interpretation that rejects the collectors and goes beyond the historians. Lesson: when the author says "only a first step," the answer that stops at that step is too narrow.

choices.note: The trap. The author agrees with this, but calls it "only a first step." Most of the passage (P3-P4) goes past deliberateness to what the offsets meant. Too narrow.
The author never ranks funeral cloths as the best. They're used to show the weavers could align and, later, as meaningful stillness. Not the purpose.
The banding process is described in one sentence of P1 as background. The passage is about interpretation, not technique.
CORRECT. The author defends the rhythm interpretation, rejects the collectors' "indifference to precision" account, and refines the historians' view: deliberate, yes, but not a fixed vocabulary.
That's the vocabulary view the author says has "thin" evidence. The author prefers rhythm, where single offsets don't carry fixed meanings.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following indicates that Kestel weavers were capable of exact alignment?
choices: Cloths made for funerals are almost perfectly matched across their seams.
The weavers had a specific term for the full reversal of a motif's direction.
Dealers' catalogues described the cloths as artless expressions of an undisciplined culture.
The same offset appears on cloths made for very different occasions.
The industrial loom achieves greater uniformity than hand weaving does.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph cites the near-perfect alignment of funeral cloths as evidence that the weavers 'were capable of exact alignment when they chose,' which is A. B is the trap: it appears in the same paragraph, but as evidence that offsets were planned and named, not that the weavers could align bands exactly. D is used for a different purpose in the third paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the evidence the passage gives that the weavers could align the bands exactly.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: P2 makes two separate points with two separate pieces of evidence. Capable of exact alignment → funeral cloths are almost perfectly matched. Offsets were planned → weavers had names for kinds of offset. The question asks about the first. Prephrase: the funeral cloths. Lesson: match the evidence to the specific claim it supports, not just to the right paragraph.

choices.note: CORRECT. P2: weavers "were capable of exact alignment when they chose. Cloths made for funerals ... are almost perfectly matched across their seams." If you can make one perfectly aligned cloth, you have the skill.
The trap. Same paragraph, different job. Named offsets show the offsets were planned, not that the weavers could line bands up exactly.
That's the collectors' view, which implies the weavers lacked precision. It's the opposite of evidence for capability.
From P3, used to cast doubt on fixed symbolic meanings. It says nothing about alignment skill.
Not in the passage as a claim about capability. The industrial loom shows up in P4 as the collectors' hidden standard.

questions.stem: The author points out that the weavers' terms for offsets 'describe their visual form rather than anything they might stand for' primarily in order to
choices: support the claim that the misalignments in Kestel cloths were deliberate rather than accidental
suggest that the last generation of weavers had forgotten the original meanings of the offsets
cast doubt on the view that each type of offset carried a fixed symbolic meaning
explain why collectors failed to recognize that the offsets were planned
concede that the view that each offset carried a fixed meaning cannot be conclusively ruled out
questions.explanation: The observation is the first reason given for the judgment that the evidence for fixed symbolic meanings 'is thin,' which is C. A is a trap because the existence of named offsets is used in the second paragraph to show deliberateness, but this remark about what the names describe serves the later argument. E is the other trap: the concession that the view is not ruled out comes in the following sentence and qualifies the remark rather than stating its purpose.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author notes that the weavers' offset terms describe visual form, not meaning.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3: "The evidence for this is thin." followed by the two reasons, then the "To be sure" concession.

breakdown.analysis: Sequence in P3: some say each offset had a fixed meaning; "The evidence for this is thin"; reason 1: the terms describe shape, not meaning; reason 2: the same offset shows up on very different occasions. So the line is a reason for doubting the vocabulary view. Prephrase: to undercut the fixed-meaning view. If every word in a language were just a description of its own letters, you'd doubt it was a language of meanings.

choices.note: Trap. In P2 the existence of named offsets supports deliberateness. But this remark is about what the names describe, and it's used in P3 against the symbolic view.
The author never suggests the weavers forgot meanings. If anything, the concession suggests meanings might have been kept from outsiders, not forgotten.
CORRECT. It's the first reason the author gives for saying the evidence for fixed symbolic meanings "is thin."
The collectors are in P1 and P4. This remark has nothing to do with why they missed the planning.
Trap. The concession comes in the next sentence ("To be sure, this does not rule the view out"), and it qualifies the remark. The remark itself pushes against the view; the concession pulls back.

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree with which one of the following statements about Kestel cloths?
choices: Each type of offset was reserved for cloths made for a particular kind of occasion.
Cloths with more offsets were valued more highly by the weavers than cloths with fewer.
The weavers adopted offsets because they lacked the means to align bands made on narrow looms.
The funeral cloths are less significant as works of art than cloths made for other occasions.
The significance of a particular offset cannot be fully determined by examining that offset in isolation.
questions.explanation: On the author's rhythmic view, what mattered was 'not what any single offset signified but the pattern of expectation and variation' across the whole cloth, so an offset's significance depends on its context, which is E. A is the trap: the funeral-cloth point might suggest occasion-specific design, but the author notes that 'the same offset appears on cloths made for very different occasions.' C restates the collectors' error, and D conflicts with the author's claim that the funeral cloths' stillness is itself significant.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement about Kestel cloths that the author would agree with.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, the rhythm view: "what mattered was not what any single offset signified but the pattern ... across the whole cloth."

breakdown.analysis: The author's own view is rhythm. In music, one note doesn't mean much by itself; it matters because of what comes before and after. Same here: an offset gets its significance from the pattern around it. Prephrase: you can't understand one offset alone. Lesson: on "would agree" questions, go to the author's own view and find the answer that restates it.

choices.note: Trap. Funeral cloths might make you think offsets were tied to occasions, but the author says "the same offset appears on cloths made for very different occasions."
Nothing about the weavers valuing more offsets over fewer. The funeral cloths, with almost none, are called significant in their own way.
This is the collectors' error. The author says the weavers could align bands when they chose, and offsets were deliberate.
Conflicts with the author. The funeral cloths' stillness is "significant precisely as an absence of rhythm." No ranking of artistic worth.

CORRECT. Under the rhythm view, what matters is "the pattern of expectation and variation that the offsets created across the whole cloth," not any single offset. So looking at one offset alone can't tell you its full significance.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the view that each type of offset carried a fixed symbolic meaning is best described as
choices: dismissive, regarding it as refuted by the evidence of the weavers' own terminology
doubtful, regarding it as poorly supported while allowing that the available evidence cannot exclude it
receptive, regarding it as plausible though not yet confirmed by the recorded instructions
evenhanded, regarding it as about as well supported as the view that the offsets functioned like rhythm
critical, regarding it as repeating the collectors' error of judging the cloths by an industrial standard
questions.explanation: The author says the evidence for the view 'is thin' and prefers the rhythmic view as 'more plausible,' yet concedes that 'this does not rule the view out,' since ritual meanings may never have been spoken to outsiders, which is B. A is the trap for readers who miss the concession: the author never claims refutation. C and D understate the author's doubt, and E transfers the author's criticism of the collectors to a view the author faults only for weak evidence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the author's attitude toward the fixed-symbolic-meaning view of offsets.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3: "The evidence for this is thin," "To be sure, this does not rule the view out," and "A more plausible view."

breakdown.analysis: Three signals: "thin" evidence (doubt), "does not rule the view out" (concession), "more plausible view" (prefers rhythm). So: skeptical but not dismissive. Prephrase: doubtful, but admits it's still possible. Lesson: attitude answers have to match the strength; "refuted" and "evenhanded" are both off by a notch in opposite directions.

choices.note: Too strong. The author explicitly says "this does not rule the view out." Dismissive and "refuted" ignore the concession.
CORRECT. "Poorly supported" = "the evidence for this is thin"; "cannot exclude it" = "does not rule the view out," since ritual meanings might never have been told to outsiders.
Too warm. The author calls the evidence thin and prefers another view as more plausible. That's not receptive.
Not evenhanded. The author calls the rhythm view "more plausible."
Wrong criticism. The industrial-standard error belongs to the collectors in P4. The author faults the symbolic view only for weak evidence.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the role that offsets play in Kestel cloths, according to the view the author favors?
choices: the arrangement of flags flown from a ship's mast, each combination of which conveys a specific, agreed-upon message to the crews of other vessels
the uneven brushstrokes of a novice painter, which reveal an unfamiliarity with the techniques taught in academies
the color coding of wires in an electrical panel, in which each color indicates a distinct circuit
the irregular spacing of columns along a colonnade, which produces alternating impressions of crowding and openness as one walks its length, though no single interval stands for anything
the decorative motifs painted on a set of ceremonial vessels, each of which identifies the particular family that commissioned that vessel
questions.explanation: The author holds that offsets mattered for the pattern of expectation and variation they created across the whole work, not for anything a single offset meant; irregular column spacing valued for its cumulative effect matches this, which is D. A is the most tempting trap because, like offsets, flag arrangements are deliberate patterns, but each combination carries a fixed meaning, which is the vocabulary view the author doubts; C and E share that feature. B matches the collectors' reading of irregularity as lack of skill.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the example where something plays the same role offsets play under the author's rhythm view.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, the rhythm comparison: significance lies in the pattern across the whole cloth, not in what any single offset stands for.

breakdown.analysis: Two features to match: (1) deliberate variation, and (2) the effect comes from the overall pattern, not from each unit meaning something. Prephrase: an intentional irregularity that creates an experience as you move through it, with no single piece standing for anything. Lesson: on analogy questions, wrong answers often match one feature (deliberate pattern) but miss the key one (no fixed meaning).

choices.note: Tempting because flag arrangements are deliberate. But each combination has a specific agreed-upon message. That's the vocabulary view the author doubts.
This is the collectors' reading: irregularity as lack of skill. The author rejects that.
Each color stands for one thing. Fixed code again, the vocabulary model.

CORRECT. Deliberately irregular spacing creates alternating crowding and openness as you walk, a pattern of expectation and variation, and "no single interval stands for anything." That's the rhythm view exactly.
Each motif identifies a family, so each unit has a fixed meaning. Vocabulary model, not rhythm.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of passage B?
choices: Evaluating mixed-income housing by the number of cross-income friendships it produces overlooks other ways in which it can benefit lower-income residents.
Mixed-income housing succeeds chiefly because lower-income residents learn about job openings through weak ties with higher-income neighbors.
Surveys that ask residents to name their friends are an unreliable method of studying any neighborhood.
Mixed-income housing is a more efficient means of improving public services in lower-income neighborhoods than direct provision by a city.
Lower-income residents of mixed-income developments form more cross-class friendships than critics have claimed.
questions.explanation: Passage B argues that the friendship-counting standard 'misconstrues how residential settings shape opportunity,' pointing to weak ties and, 'more important,' institutional improvements, which is A. D is the trap: passage B explicitly says that nothing it presents 'shows that mixed-income housing is the most efficient way to secure such improvements.' B is too narrow, since the author ranks the institutional channel above weak ties, and E contradicts the concession that by the friendship measure such housing 'frequently disappoints.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the main point of passage B only.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first paragraph ("this standard misconstrues how residential settings shape opportunity") and the last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Passage B's claim: counting cross-class friendships is the wrong yardstick. It misses weak ties and, more important, institutional gains like better services. B even admits mixed-income housing disappoints by the friendship measure and that it may not be the most efficient route. Prephrase: judging by friendships misses other real benefits. Lesson: watch for answers that take a passage's careful claim ("must take them into account") and inflate it ("more efficient," "succeeds chiefly").

choices.note: CORRECT. This is B's thesis: the friendship standard "misconstrues how residential settings shape opportunity," and a fair assessment must count the gains through weak ties and institutions.
Too narrow and wrongly ranked. Weak ties are one channel; the author says "more important" is the institutional channel. B also never claims the housing "succeeds chiefly" at all.
Too broad. B says friend-naming surveys miss weak ties in this context. It never says such surveys are unreliable for studying any neighborhood.
The trap. B explicitly says none of this "shows that mixed-income housing is the most efficient way" and that a city "could in principle provide them directly."
Contradicts B's concession that by the friendship measure such housing "frequently disappoints." B doesn't dispute the friendship counts; it disputes the measure.

questions.stem: According to passage A, conversations between residents of different income groups at Linden Court
choices: led to job referrals for some lower-income residents
gave rise to friendships mainly after residents had lived there for several years
took place mainly in neighborhood shops and clinics
were more common among residents who had children
were mostly brief and concerned practical matters
questions.explanation: Passage A states that cross-group conversations 'were mostly brief and concerned practical matters such as parking and noise,' which is E. B is the trap: it reverses Arquero's reply to the advocates, which is that the few cross-group friendships 'had all formed within the first year' and none formed thereafter. A describes the kind of benefit passage B discusses in general, not something passage A reports from Linden Court.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A says about cross-income conversations at Linden Court.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, first paragraph, the sentence about Arquero's findings.

breakdown.analysis: Straight detail. Arquero found friendships formed mostly within income groups, and "conversations across groups were mostly brief and concerned practical matters such as parking and noise." Prephrase: short and practical. Lesson: be careful with answers that pull in passage B's ideas when the question asks about passage A.

choices.note: Passage A reports nothing about job referrals at Linden Court. Job information flowing through weak ties is passage B's general idea.
Reversed. Arquero found the few cross-group friendships "had all formed within the first year," and none formed after.
Passage A mentions shops and clinics only to say lower-income tenants use them. It never says cross-group conversations happened there.
Children come up only in where higher-income parents send them to school. Nothing about conversation frequency.
CORRECT. Near-verbatim: conversations across groups "were mostly brief and concerned practical matters such as parking and noise."

questions.stem: Passage A suggests that the tendency of residents of different incomes to use different stores and schools
choices: is the main reason that mixed-income developments are costly to build
results from deliberate efforts by higher-income residents to avoid their neighbors
reduces the opportunities for the kind of contact through which relationships are formed
would diminish if residents were given more than five years to become acquainted
has diminished as mixed-income developments have become more established
questions.explanation: Passage A's second paragraph holds that relationships form 'through repeated, purposeful contact'; combined with the first paragraph's observation that residents of different incomes use different spaces, this implies few occasions for such contact, which is C. B is the trap: it supplies a motive, deliberate avoidance, that the passage never attributes. D borrows the advocates' five-year argument, which Arquero answers with evidence that friendships did not form later.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Figure out what passage A implies about residents of different incomes using different stores and schools.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, end of the first paragraph (different spaces) together with the second paragraph ("People form relationships through repeated, purposeful contact").

breakdown.analysis: Connect the two paragraphs. Relationships come from repeated, purposeful contact. Higher- and lower-income residents shop, school, and get care in different places. So they rarely run into each other in the ways that build ties. Prephrase: fewer chances for relationship-building contact. Think of two coworkers on different floors with different lunch spots; they share an employer but never really meet.

choices.note: Construction costs come up only in the recommendation. Nothing ties them to shopping and school choices.
The trap. Passage A never gives a motive. Higher-income tenants may drive to stores out of convenience, not to avoid neighbors. Don't invent intent.

CORRECT. Using different spaces means less of the "repeated, purposeful contact" through which, per passage A, relationships form. That's why the observation sits in an argument that proximity alone doesn't produce ties.
Borrows the advocates' five-year point, which Arquero answers: no friendships formed after the first year. Passage A suggests more time wouldn't help.
No evidence of change over time. Passage A describes the pattern as ongoing, not shrinking.

questions.stem: The author of passage B mentions the Harrow Street redevelopment primarily in order to
