choices: show that lower-income residents can successfully press local officials for improved services
support a claim about the channel through which a mixed neighborhood principally exerts its influence
provide an example of weak ties transmitting information about employment
show that mixed-income housing secures public improvements more efficiently than direct provision would
demonstrate that cross-class friendships are more common than surveys of residents indicate
questions.explanation: Harrow Street is offered as evidence for the claim that a mixed neighborhood's influence 'operates largely through institutions rather than through individual relationships,' which is B. A reverses the example's point, since longtime residents had requested the improvements 'for a decade without success.' D is the other trap: passage B disclaims any showing that mixed-income housing is 'the most efficient way' to secure such improvements.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why passage B brings up the Harrow Street redevelopment.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph: its first sentence ("operates largely through institutions") and the Harrow Street sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The paragraph opens with a claim: a mixed neighborhood's influence works mainly through institutions, not personal relationships. Then Harrow Street: higher-income tenants arrive, and within three years there's better bus service and a renovated library that longtime residents had wanted for a decade. That's an example backing the claim. Prephrase: evidence for the institutional channel. Lesson: an example usually supports the general claim right before it.

choices.note: Opposite of the point. Longtime residents had asked "for a decade without success." The improvements came after higher-income tenants arrived.
CORRECT. It's evidence for the paragraph's opening claim that a mixed neighborhood's influence "operates largely through institutions rather than through individual relationships."
Weak ties are in the first paragraph of passage B. Harrow Street is about services and institutions, not job tips between neighbors.
The trap. B immediately says none of this shows mixed-income housing is "the most efficient way" to get such improvements.
B doesn't claim cross-class friendships are more common; the improvements happened whether or not anyone talked to their neighbors.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between passage A and passage B?
choices: Passage B presents evidence that confirms the conclusion reached in passage A while drawing a different policy recommendation from it.
Passage A proposes a policy that passage B argues would be too costly to implement.
Passage B offers a historical account of a policy whose present-day effects passage A evaluates.
Passage B challenges the standard of evaluation on which passage A's negative assessment of a policy depends.
Passage A and passage B rely on the same study but reach opposing interpretations of its findings.
questions.explanation: Passage A judges mixed-income housing by whether it produces cross-income relationships and finds it wanting; passage B argues that judging such housing by counting friendships 'misconstrues how residential settings shape opportunity,' which is D. A is the trap: passage B accepts passage A's friendship data, but it rejects rather than confirms passage A's overall negative conclusion. E fails because the passages cite different developments.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B relates to passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A's standard (cross-income ties) and conclusion (proximity doesn't create ties, so fund other programs); passage B's first paragraph attacking that standard.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A judges mixed-income housing by whether it builds relationships across income lines and finds it lacking. Passage B says that's the wrong test: much of the benefit comes through weak ties and institutions. B doesn't dispute A's facts; it disputes the yardstick. Prephrase: B attacks the measure A's negative verdict relies on. It's like one critic saying a car is bad because it's slow and another saying speed isn't what a family car should be judged on.

choices.note: The trap. B accepts A's friendship data, but it doesn't confirm A's conclusion that the policy rests on an unrealistic picture. B rejects that overall negative assessment.
A's proposal (mentoring, job placement) isn't discussed by B at all, let alone called too costly. A is the one complaining about cost.
B isn't historical. Both evaluate present-day effects.
CORRECT. A's negative verdict depends on measuring success by cross-income relationships. B says that standard "misconstrues how residential settings shape opportunity."
Different studies: A uses Linden Court, B uses Harrow Street.

questions.stem: The authors of both passages would most likely agree that
choices: close friendships between residents of different incomes are relatively uncommon in mixed-income developments
mixed-income housing should be replaced by programs that create purposeful contact between income groups
weak ties between neighbors are an important source of information about employment
the presence of higher-income households tends to improve the public services available to a neighborhood
public services in lower-income neighborhoods could in principle be improved without mixed-income housing
questions.explanation: Passage A reports that friendships formed 'overwhelmingly within' income groups, and passage B concedes that by the friendship measure such housing 'frequently disappoints,' so both accept A. E is the trap: passage B says a city 'could in principle provide them directly,' but passage A never discusses public services, so there is no basis for attributing the view to its author. B is passage A's position alone, and C and D are claims only passage B makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim both authors would accept.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A's Linden Court findings; passage B's first sentence ("by that measure it frequently disappoints").

breakdown.analysis: Look for overlap. A: friendships formed overwhelmingly within income groups. B: by the friendship count, mixed-income housing "frequently disappoints." So both accept that close cross-income friendships are rare. Prephrase: cross-class friendships are uncommon. Lesson: on agreement questions, both authors must have actually spoken to the claim; one saying it and the other being silent isn't agreement.

choices.note: CORRECT. A finds friendships form overwhelmingly within income groups. B concedes the friendship measure "frequently disappoints." Both accept that close cross-income friendships are relatively uncommon.
Only A's view, and even A says resources "might be better directed," not that housing should be replaced. B wants the housing's benefits counted.
Only B makes the weak-ties claim. A never discusses weak ties.
Only B. A never talks about public services improving.
The trap. B says a city "could in principle provide them directly," but A never discusses public services, so there's no basis to say A's author agrees.

questions.stem: Passage A's observation about where higher-income tenants enroll their children bears on passage B's argument in which one of the following ways?
choices: It supports passage B's claim that weak ties between neighbors are easily missed by surveys.
It supports passage B's claim that officials respond most readily to residents who vote and organize.
It undermines passage B's claim that critics measure mixed-income housing by counting friendships.
It confirms passage B's claim that higher-income households press officials for improved public services.
It suggests a limit on passage B's claim that lower-income residents share in service improvements prompted by higher-income neighbors.
questions.explanation: Passage B's institutional argument assumes that higher-income households press for services both groups use; if they send their children to private schools while lower-income tenants rely on neighborhood schools, they have little reason to press for better neighborhood schools, so the shared benefit may not extend to every service, which is E. D is the trap: the observation is at most consistent with advocacy for parks and streets and confirms nothing about it; its bearing is to expose a service where the two groups' interests diverge. B and C link the observation to claims it does not affect.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Figure out how passage A's point about higher-income tenants using private schools affects passage B's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, last sentence of the first paragraph; passage B, second paragraph (higher-income households press for services lower-income residents share).

breakdown.analysis: B's institutional argument: wealthier residents lobby for better services, and everyone benefits. That only works for services both groups actually use. A says higher-income tenants send kids to private schools while lower-income tenants use neighborhood schools. So wealthier residents have little reason to push for better neighborhood schools. Prephrase: it shows a service where the shared-benefit story may break down. It's like expecting the neighbor with a private pool to lobby for a better public pool.

choices.note: School choice has nothing to do with whether surveys catch weak ties.
Nothing about school enrollment bears on whether officials respond to voters and organizers.
A's observation doesn't touch how critics measure success. And passage A itself is an example of measuring by relationships, so it wouldn't undermine B's description.
The trap. Private-school enrollment confirms nothing about lobbying. At most it's consistent with lobbying for parks or streets; its real bearing is pointing to a service where interests split.

CORRECT. B assumes higher-income residents push for services both groups use. If they don't use neighborhood schools, they likely won't push for them, so lower-income residents may not share in improvements there. It limits B's claim without refuting it.

questions.stimulus: Some researchers have proposed relocating the threatened coral colonies of the Calloway reef to the cooler waters off Pemmer Point, but this proposal should be abandoned. Its supporters point out, correctly, that the waters off Pemmer Point would shield the corals from the heat stress now bleaching them. Yet the point lies in the path of seasonal storms whose surge regularly scours the seabed, so transplanted corals would probably be torn loose within a few years. And the money the project would consume could instead fund efforts to curb the runoff pollution that is also degrading the Calloway reef.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: The waters off Pemmer Point would shield transplanted corals from the heat stress that is bleaching them.
Corals transplanted to Pemmer Point would probably be torn loose by storm surge within a few years.
The proposal to relocate the Calloway reef's coral colonies to Pemmer Point should not be pursued.
The money for the relocation would be better spent curbing runoff pollution at the Calloway reef.
Storm surge poses a greater threat to coral colonies than heat stress does.
questions.explanation: The conclusion appears in the first sentence: the proposal should be abandoned, and every later sentence gives a reason for that, so C is correct. B is the most tempting trap: it is itself supported (by the claim about storm surge), but it is offered as a reason for abandoning the proposal, not as the point being argued for; A is a concession, and D restates a supporting premise.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The proposal to relocate the Calloway reef's corals to Pemmer Point should be abandoned.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pemmer Point is in the path of storms whose surge would likely tear corals loose within a few years; the money could instead fund efforts to curb runoff pollution at Calloway.

breakdown.analysis: The conclusion is up front: abandon the proposal. Everything after is support. There's a concession (yes, Pemmer Point would shield corals from heat), then two reasons against: storms would rip the corals loose, and the money has a better use. Lesson: a conclusion in the first sentence followed by 'Yet' and 'And' reasons is a common structure. Don't let the most vivid premise steal the spotlight.

choices.note: This is the concession to the supporters ('correctly'). The author grants it, then argues past it.
The most tempting trap. It has its own support (storm surge scours the seabed), but it's offered as a reason to abandon the proposal. It serves the conclusion.
CORRECT. 'Should not be pursued' is the same as 'should be abandoned.' Every other sentence is a reason for this.
A supporting premise: the money could fund pollution efforts instead. It's a reason to abandon the relocation, not the main point.
The author never compares the general threat of storms with heat stress. It's a claim about Pemmer Point specifically, and even then it's a premise.

questions.stimulus: Councilor Ferro opposes the proposal to raise the city's road-maintenance budget. He argues that the poor condition of the city's roads stems from lax oversight of paving contractors rather than from underfunding, and he cites a state audit that found repeated billing irregularities by those contractors. But Ferro owns a trucking business that would pay higher vehicle fees if the proposal were adopted. So his argument against the proposal should be rejected.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: rejects an argument because of a fact about the person advancing it rather than by addressing the argument's merits
takes for granted that the state audit Ferro cites was conducted competently and without bias
presumes that underfunding and lax oversight could not both contribute to the condition of the roads
concludes that the proposal should be adopted merely because one argument against it is unpersuasive
relies on a claim about vehicle fees that is inconsistent with other claims made in the argument
questions.explanation: The argument dismisses Ferro's reasoning solely by pointing to his financial interest, never engaging his evidence, so A is correct. D is the tempting trap: the argument concludes only that Ferro's argument should be rejected, not that the proposal should be adopted; C describes a possible weakness in Ferro's reasoning, not in the argument being evaluated.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ferro's argument against the road-budget proposal should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ferro owns a trucking business that would pay higher vehicle fees if the proposal passed.

breakdown.analysis: Ferro gave an actual argument with evidence (a state audit). The author ignores all of it and attacks Ferro's motives. That's ad hominem. Having a stake doesn't make your argument wrong. It's like dismissing a dentist's advice to floss because she makes money from your teeth. The advice might still be right.

choices.note: CORRECT. The only reason given for rejecting Ferro's argument is his financial interest. The audit evidence and his reasoning are never addressed.
The author doesn't rely on the audit at all; that's Ferro's evidence. The author's argument takes nothing about the audit for granted.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: A state audit found billing problems, so the contractors are clearly corrupt.

choices.note: This might be a weakness in Ferro's reasoning, not in the author's. The author never engages whether roads suffer from both causes.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The roads are bad because of lax oversight, so funding can't have anything to do with it.

choices.note: The trap. The author only concludes that Ferro's argument should be rejected, not that the proposal should be adopted.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Ferro's argument against the budget increase fails, so the city should raise the budget.

choices.note: Nothing in the argument contradicts the claim about vehicle fees. No inconsistency.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The proposal won't cost drivers anything. Also, it will raise vehicle fees for truckers.

questions.stimulus: Dunmore Regional Airport's managers expected fewer departures to be delayed by aircraft de-icing this past winter, because the season brought considerably fewer days of freezing rain or snow, the only conditions that make de-icing necessary, than the previous winter did. Instead, the airport's records show that the number of departures delayed by de-icing was substantially higher this past winter than in the previous one.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Most departures delayed at Dunmore this past winter were delayed for reasons unrelated to weather.
Freezing rain, rather than snow, is the condition that most often requires aircraft at Dunmore to be de-iced.
Several other regional airports also reported more de-icing delays this past winter than in the previous one.
Before this past winter, Dunmore replaced its de-icing equipment with a system that takes much longer per aircraft.
On several days of freezing rain this past winter, departures at Dunmore were canceled outright rather than delayed.
questions.explanation: If each aircraft now takes much longer to de-ice, fewer icing days could still produce more delayed departures, so D resolves the puzzle. E points the wrong way: cancellations this past winter would lower the count of delayed departures, deepening the discrepancy; C merely shows that the puzzle also exists elsewhere.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: This winter had far fewer freezing rain or snow days (the only conditions needing de-icing), but more departures were delayed by de-icing.

breakdown.analysis: Fewer icing days, more de-icing delays. Something must have made each icing day worse, or each de-icing slower. Prephrase: the de-icing process itself got slower, or each icing day affected more flights. It's like having fewer rainy days but getting soaked more often because your umbrella broke.

choices.note: The puzzle is specifically about de-icing delays. Other delays are irrelevant.
Which kind of weather causes most de-icing doesn't explain why fewer icing days led to more delays. We'd need to know the mix changed, and we aren't told that.
Shows the puzzle happened elsewhere too. That doesn't resolve it; it just spreads it around.
CORRECT. If the new system takes much longer per aircraft, each icing day can back up many more departures. Fewer days, but more delays per day. Both facts fit.
Points the wrong way. Cancellations remove flights from the delayed count, so this makes the higher delay number even more puzzling.

questions.stimulus: In a large survey, adults who ate at least one serving of fermented vegetables daily had significantly lower average blood levels of a marker of inflammation than did adults who rarely ate fermented vegetables, even after the researchers adjusted their comparison for differences in age and income. On the basis of this finding, the researchers concluded that eating fermented vegetables reduces inflammation in adults.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Adults who eat fermented vegetables daily also tend to eat more fresh fruit, which is associated with lower inflammation.
In a later trial, adults randomly assigned to add a daily serving of fermented vegetables showed declines in the marker.
Fermented vegetables contain bacteria that some researchers believe may affect the human digestive system.
The blood marker used in the survey is also elevated in people who have recently had a minor infection.
Many adults who rarely eat fermented vegetables report that they dislike the taste of such foods.
questions.explanation: The survey shows only a correlation; B supplies a randomized intervention in which adding fermented vegetables was followed by lower marker levels, directly supporting causation. C is the tempting trap: it hints at a mechanism, but 'may affect the digestive system' says nothing about inflammation; A weakens the argument by offering an alternative cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Eating fermented vegetables reduces inflammation in adults.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a survey, daily fermented-vegetable eaters had lower inflammation markers than those who rarely ate them, even after adjusting for age and income.

breakdown.analysis: Survey data is correlation. Maybe fermented-vegetable eaters exercise more, eat better overall, or smoke less. Age and income adjustments don't cover everything. The gold standard to strengthen a causal claim is an experiment: randomly assign people to the food and see if the marker drops. Randomization washes out the 'they were different to begin with' problem.

choices.note: This weakens. Fresh fruit is an alternative explanation for the lower inflammation.
CORRECT. A randomized trial where adding fermented vegetables was followed by marker declines directly supports causation and rules out self-selection.
The tempting trap. 'May affect the digestive system' is vague and says nothing about inflammation. A hint of a mechanism isn't a mechanism.
If anything this raises a worry (infections could confound the comparison), but it doesn't say the groups differed in infection rates. It doesn't strengthen.
Why people avoid fermented vegetables (taste) has nothing to do with whether eating them reduces inflammation.

questions.stimulus: Every bird species that nests on Tavish Island spends the winter along the mainland coast. No species that winters along the mainland coast feeds primarily on insects unless it also forages in salt marshes. None of the species that forage in salt marshes is protected under the regional wildlife statute. Some of the species that nest on Tavish Island are protected under that statute.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: No species that feeds primarily on insects is protected under the regional wildlife statute.
Every species that nests on Tavish Island and forages in salt marshes feeds primarily on insects.
Some species that nest on Tavish Island forage in salt marshes.
No species that nests on Tavish Island feeds primarily on insects.
Some species protected under the regional wildlife statute do not feed primarily on insects.
questions.explanation: The protected Tavish nesters winter on the mainland coast and, being protected, do not forage in salt marshes; a mainland-wintering species that does not forage in salt marshes cannot feed primarily on insects, so E follows. D is the trap: Tavish nesters that do forage in salt marshes (and are unprotected) may feed on insects. A fails because protected insect-eaters that never winter on the mainland coast are not ruled out.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Tavish nester → winters on mainland coast; 2) winters on mainland coast AND feeds on insects → forages in salt marshes; 3) forages in salt marshes → NOT protected; 4) some Tavish nesters are protected.

breakdown.analysis: Follow the protected Tavish nesters from fact 4. They winter on the mainland (fact 1). They're protected, so they don't forage in salt marshes (contrapositive of 3). A mainland winterer that doesn't forage in salt marshes can't feed primarily on insects (contrapositive of 2). So those protected species don't feed primarily on insects. That gives: some protected species don't feed primarily on insects.

choices.note: Too broad. The chain only works for species that winter on the mainland coast. A protected insect-eater that winters somewhere else isn't ruled out.
Reverses fact 2. Insect-eaters (among mainland winterers) must forage in salt marshes, but salt-marsh foragers needn't be insect-eaters.
Possible but not required. Nothing says any Tavish nester forages in salt marshes.
The trap. The protected Tavish nesters can't be insect-eaters, but unprotected Tavish nesters that forage in salt marshes could feed on insects. 'No Tavish nester' is too strong.

CORRECT. The protected Tavish nesters winter on the mainland, can't forage in salt marshes (they're protected), and so can't feed primarily on insects. They're protected species that don't feed on insects.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago, the Corland school district began requiring that every teacher be given ninety minutes of planning time each school day. Since then, the average score of Corland students on the statewide mathematics examination has risen considerably, after being flat for the preceding decade. The district superintendent therefore concludes that the additional planning time is responsible for the improvement.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Teachers in Corland used most of their additional planning time to prepare mathematics lessons.
No other school district in the state adopted a similar planning-time requirement during the period.
The statewide mathematics examination was not made substantially easier over the past two years.
Average scores of Corland students on examinations in other subjects have also risen since the requirement began.
Average mathematics scores in Corland would have continued to rise even without the planning-time requirement.
questions.explanation: If the examination had become substantially easier, the rise would be explained without the planning time, so the argument requires C. A is the tempting trap: planning time spent on general instruction could still raise mathematics scores, so A is not required. E is the opposite of what the argument needs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The extra planning time is responsible for the rise in Corland students' math scores.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Two years ago Corland required 90 minutes of daily planning time; since then, average math scores rose considerably after a decade of being flat.

breakdown.analysis: Timing-based causation: A happened, then B happened, so A caused B. The argument has to assume no other explanation accounts for the rise. One obvious alternative: the test itself got easier. That's like crediting your new diet for weight loss when your scale was recalibrated the same week.

choices.note: The tempting trap. Negate it: teachers spent most of the time on other things (general planning, grading). Better general teaching could still raise math scores. The argument survives, so it's not required.
choices.negation: Teachers in Corland did not use most of their additional planning time to prepare mathematics lessons.

choices.note: Negate it: another district adopted a similar requirement. That says nothing about whether the requirement explains Corland's scores. No damage.
choices.negation: At least one other school district in the state adopted a similar planning-time requirement during the period.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the exam was made substantially easier. Then the score rise has a different explanation, and the argument collapses. Required.
choices.negation: The statewide mathematics examination was made substantially easier over the past two years.

choices.note: Negate it: scores in other subjects didn't rise. The argument is only about math, so it doesn't need other subjects to improve. No damage.
choices.negation: Average scores of Corland students on examinations in other subjects have not also risen since the requirement began.

choices.note: The opposite of what the argument needs. If scores would have risen anyway, the requirement isn't responsible. Negating it actually helps the argument.
choices.negation: Average mathematics scores in Corland would not have continued to rise without the planning-time requirement.

questions.stimulus:
Okafor: The novelist Lise Varnay's late works are weaker than her early ones. Her early novels were admired for their spare, exact prose, but in the late novels the sentences sprawl and whole chapters pass without advancing the plot.

Halvorsen: The sprawl you describe is deliberate. In her late novels Varnay was exploring how memory resists orderly narration, and their loose structure enacts that theme. Judged by what she was attempting, those novels are her finest achievements.
questions.stem: Okafor and Halvorsen disagree over whether
choices: Varnay's late novels are artistically inferior to her early novels
the sentences in Varnay's late novels are looser than those in her early novels
Varnay deliberately chose the loose structure of her late novels
the structure of a novel can reflect the novel's central themes
Varnay's early novels were admired for the quality of their prose
questions.explanation: Okafor says the late works are weaker; Halvorsen says they are her finest achievements, so they disagree about A. C is the most tempting trap: Halvorsen asserts the sprawl is deliberate, but Okafor never says it was accidental, so Okafor's view on C is unknown. B fails because Halvorsen accepts the description of sprawl.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Okafor: Varnay's late novels are weaker than her early ones, with sprawling sentences and chapters that don't advance the plot.; Halvorsen: The sprawl is deliberate, enacting the theme of memory; judged by her aims, the late novels are her finest.

breakdown.analysis: Okafor says the late works are weaker. Halvorsen says they're her finest achievements. That's a clean disagreement about quality. Both agree the late books sprawl; they disagree on whether that's a weakness. Lesson: to disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no.

choices.note: CORRECT. Okafor: yes, the late novels are weaker. Halvorsen: no, they're her finest achievements. Clear yes/no split.
Halvorsen accepts the description ('the sprawl you describe'). They agree here.
The most tempting trap. Halvorsen says the sprawl is deliberate, but Okafor never says it was accidental. She might well think it was intentional and still bad. No view from her.
Halvorsen implies yes. Okafor never addresses whether structure can reflect theme. One opinion only.
Okafor says this; Halvorsen doesn't dispute it or address it. No disagreement.

questions.stimulus: An analyst at Brightway Mutual, an auto insurer, found that policyholders who had chosen to install the company's optional dashboard driving monitor filed 30 percent fewer claims last year than policyholders who had not, even though the two groups were similar in average age and in the value of their vehicles. The analyst concluded that requiring all Brightway policyholders to install the monitor would substantially reduce the number of claims the company receives.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: presumes without justification that the monitor is the only device capable of reducing claims
fails to consider that some claims are filed for damage that occurs while vehicles are parked
takes for granted that the number of claims filed is a reliable indicator of the total cost of claims
relies on data from a single year without establishing that the year was typical
overlooks the possibility that drivers who chose to install the monitor differ in their habits from those who did not
questions.explanation: Drivers who volunteer for a monitor may already be more cautious, and matching the groups on age and vehicle value does not address that, so E identifies the flaw. C is the trap: the conclusion concerns the number of claims, not their cost, so the argument makes no such assumption; D is a minor concern that does not touch the self-selection gap.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Requiring all policyholders to install the monitor would substantially reduce claims.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Policyholders who chose to install the monitor filed 30% fewer claims than those who didn't; the groups were similar in age and vehicle value.

breakdown.analysis: Self-selection. The people who volunteered to have their driving monitored are probably careful drivers to begin with. Who signs up to be watched? People who aren't worried about what the camera will see. Matching on age and car value doesn't fix that. Forcing the monitor on everyone else might not change how they drive at all.

choices.note: The argument doesn't need the monitor to be the only claim-reducing device; it just says the monitor would help.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Monitors reduce claims, so there's no point in offering safe-driver courses.

choices.note: Parked-car claims might not be affected by a monitor, but that wouldn't undermine a 'substantial' reduction overall. Not the core problem.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The monitor will cut every kind of claim, including damage from hail while the car sits in a garage.

choices.note: The trap. The conclusion is about the number of claims, not their cost. The argument never assumes anything about cost.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We received fewer claims this year, so our payouts must have dropped.

choices.note: A minor quibble. Even with a typical year, the self-selection problem would remain. It doesn't touch the real gap.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Claims fell 30% last year, so they'll fall 30% every year.

choices.note: CORRECT. The people who chose the monitor may already drive more carefully. That explains the 30% gap without the monitor doing anything, so requiring it may not reduce claims.

questions.stimulus: Researchers studying the hooded wren found that males that sang more complex songs attracted mates earlier in the breeding season than other males did. However, the males with the most complex songs also spent the most time singing each day, and time spent singing reduces the time available for foraging. In years when food was scarce, these males were in poorer physical condition by the end of the season than were males with simpler songs.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Female hooded wrens prefer males in good physical condition to males with complex songs.
Singing complex songs can carry a cost for male hooded wrens under some conditions.
When food is scarce, males with simpler songs attract mates earlier than males with complex songs.
The complexity of a male hooded wren's song depends mainly on the food available to it.
Male hooded wrens with complex songs produce fewer offspring in years when food is scarce.
questions.explanation: Complex singers spend more time singing, which cuts into foraging, and in lean years they ended the season in poorer condition, which supports B's modest claim of a cost under some conditions. E is the tempting trap: poorer condition need not mean fewer offspring, and offspring are never mentioned. C is unsupported because no reversal in mating timing is reported.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Males with more complex songs attracted mates earlier; 2) they also spent the most time singing, which cuts foraging time; 3) in food-scarce years, they ended the season in poorer condition than simpler-song males.

breakdown.analysis: Complex song has a benefit (earlier mates) and a cost in lean years (worse physical condition). The safest supported answer just says singing complex songs can cost something sometimes. Lesson: on most-strongly-supported questions, the modest answer that stays inside the facts usually wins.

choices.note: The facts say complex songs attracted mates earlier. Nothing compares female preference for condition versus song.
CORRECT. Complex singers spend more time singing, less foraging, and in scarce-food years end in poorer condition. That's a cost under some conditions. Modest and directly supported.
No reversal in mating timing is reported for lean years. The poorer condition comes at the end of the season, after mating.
Nothing says food determines song complexity. The causation runs the other way in the facts: song time affects foraging.
The tempting trap. Poorer condition doesn't necessarily mean fewer offspring, and offspring are never mentioned. You can't pick an answer on a possibility.

questions.stimulus: Marlow City has begun charging a fee for curbside collection of bulky items such as furniture and appliances, a service it previously provided free. The city's budget office multiplied the number of bulky-item pickups performed last year by the new fee and arrived at a figure of $400,000. On this basis, the office projects that the fee will add about $400,000 to the city's annual revenue.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the budget office's argument?
choices: The fee Marlow City charges is lower than what private haulers in the area charge for the same service.
The number of bulky-item pickups performed last year was close to the average for the preceding five years.
Collecting and processing the new fees will require some additional administrative work by city staff.
Most items collected curbside last year could instead have been left, at no charge, at a drop-off site the city runs.
Many residents who used the service last year did so because they were moving, and the city's population is stable.
questions.explanation: The projection assumes residents will keep requesting pickups at last year's rate once they must pay; D shows that most of them have a free alternative, so demand, and thus revenue, is likely to fall well short. C is the tempting trap: added administrative costs reduce the city's net gain but not the revenue the fee brings in, which is all the projection addresses; A and B, if anything, support the projection.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new bulky-item fee will add about $400,000 to Marlow City's annual revenue.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last year's number of bulky-item pickups multiplied by the new fee equals $400,000.

breakdown.analysis: The projection assumes people will keep requesting pickups at the same rate even though it's no longer free. That's a big assumption. Charge for something that used to be free and demand drops, especially if there's a free alternative. It's like a café starting to charge for water and assuming everyone will still order it, when there's a free fountain by the door.

choices.note: If the city's fee is cheaper than private haulers, residents are more likely to keep using the city. That supports the projection, if anything.
Says last year was typical. That makes the baseline number more reliable, so it supports the projection.
The trap. Extra admin work cuts into the city's net gain, but the projection is about revenue, not profit. Revenue is untouched.
CORRECT. Most of last year's items could have gone to a free drop-off site. Once pickup costs money, many residents will likely switch, so pickups and revenue will fall well short of $400,000.
Hints that last year's movers might not repeat, but a stable population still has people moving every year. Too vague to undermine the projection seriously.

questions.stimulus: An insurer is justified in denying a claim on the grounds that the policyholder failed to disclose some information only if that information was specifically requested on the insurance application and would have affected either the insurer's decision to issue the policy or the premium it charged. Moreover, even when both of these conditions are met, such a denial is justified only if the policyholder knew the information at the time of applying.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Petrova's insurer was not justified in denying her claim for water damage on the grounds that she failed to mention an earlier leak, since the application never asked about earlier leaks.
Ames's insurer was justified in denying his claim because he knowingly failed to disclose a prior conviction the application asked about, though it would not have affected his premium.
Chen's insurer was justified in denying her claim, since she knowingly failed to disclose a medical condition that the application specifically asked about and that would have raised her premium.
Okoye's insurer was not justified in denying his claim, since the information he failed to disclose had no connection to the loss for which he filed the claim.
Delgado's insurer was justified in denying her claim, since she knew of a structural defect when she applied and the defect would have raised her premium, though the application never asked about it.
questions.explanation: The principle lists only necessary conditions; in A the information was never requested, so a necessary condition fails and the denial was not justified, exactly as the principle requires. C is the main trap: it treats the three conditions as sufficient for justification, which an 'only if' principle never establishes. B and E each call a denial justified even though a necessary condition (an effect on the premium in B, a specific request in E) is missing, so they contradict the principle.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Denial for nondisclosure is justified → the info was specifically requested AND would have affected issuance or premium AND the policyholder knew it when applying. Contrapositive: any of those missing → denial NOT justified.

breakdown.analysis: This principle only lists necessary conditions ('only if'). So it can tell you when a denial is NOT justified (a condition fails), but it can never tell you a denial IS justified. Any answer concluding 'justified' is out. Look for 'not justified' because a listed condition fails. Lesson: an 'only if' rule gives you requirements, not a guarantee.

choices.note: CORRECT. Earlier leaks were never asked about on the application, so the 'specifically requested' condition fails. By the contrapositive, the denial isn't justified.
Concludes 'justified,' which the principle never allows. Worse, the conviction wouldn't have affected the premium, and the answer doesn't say it affected issuance, so a condition may fail outright.
The main trap. All three conditions are met, but meeting necessary conditions doesn't make the denial justified. The principle never says when a denial IS justified.
Relevance to the loss isn't one of the principle's conditions. The principle can't support this reasoning.
Concludes 'justified' even though the application never asked about the defect. A necessary condition fails, so the principle says the opposite: not justified.

questions.stimulus: A manufacturer hopes to sell its new Halcyon 400 jet to airlines for use on transoceanic routes. However, airlines will not buy an aircraft for such routes unless it is certified for extended overwater flight, and no aircraft is so certified except one whose engines have passed the new reliability test. The Halcyon 400 is powered by engines designed by Varro Dynamics. Therefore, airlines will not buy the Halcyon 400 for transoceanic routes.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every aircraft whose engines pass the new reliability test is certified for extended overwater flight.
Engines designed by Varro Dynamics have failed earlier versions of the reliability test.
No engine designed by Varro Dynamics can pass the new reliability test.
Any aircraft whose engines fail the new reliability test will be denied certification for extended overwater flight.
If the Halcyon 400 is certified for extended overwater flight, airlines will buy it for transoceanic routes.
questions.explanation: Purchase requires certification, which requires engines that passed the test; if no Varro engine can pass, the Halcyon 400 cannot be certified and so will not be bought, making C sufficient. D is the most tempting trap: it merely restates the contrapositive of a premise and never establishes that the Halcyon's engines fail; A and E reverse the stated conditionals.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Airlines will not buy the Halcyon 400 for transoceanic routes.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Bought for transoceanic routes → certified for overwater flight; certified → engines passed the new reliability test; the Halcyon 400 uses Varro Dynamics engines.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: bought → certified → engines passed test. Contrapositive: engines didn't pass → not certified → not bought. So we need: the Halcyon's engines don't (can't) pass the test. The only thing we know about its engines is that Varro designed them. Bridge it: Varro engine → can't pass. Then Halcyon → not passed → not certified → not bought.

choices.note: Reverses the second conditional (passed → certified). Even if true, it doesn't tell us the Halcyon's engines fail, so nothing about purchase follows.
Failing earlier versions doesn't mean failing the new test. Too weak to guarantee anything.
CORRECT. Varro engine → can't pass the test → not certified → not bought. Every link is now in place, and the conclusion is guaranteed.
The most tempting trap. It's just the contrapositive of a premise we already have (certified → passed). It never says the Halcyon's engines actually fail, which is the missing piece.
Reverses the first conditional (certified → bought). It's about when airlines would buy, and doesn't help prove they won't.

questions.stimulus: Some critics dismiss the nineteenth-century serialized novel as a commercial product shaped by the demands of magazine publishers rather than by artistic vision. It is true that serial publication imposed constraints: each monthly installment had to end in a way that would bring readers back. But constraints are not inherently opposed to artistry. The sonnet's fourteen lines are a constraint, too, yet no one concludes that sonnets cannot be works of art. Thus, the conditions under which serialized novels were produced do not by themselves show that those novels lack artistic merit.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that constraints are not inherently opposed to artistry?
choices: It is the overall conclusion that the argument is intended to establish.
It is a premise that the critics mentioned in the argument use to support their view.
It is a concession to the critics that the argument goes on to qualify.
It is a general principle offered to illustrate the particular case of the sonnet.
It is supported by an analogy and in turn offers support for the argument's main conclusion.
questions.explanation: The sonnet comparison supports the claim about constraints, and that claim in turn supports the final 'Thus' sentence about serialized novels, so it is an intermediate conclusion, as E says. A is the main trap: the claim is a conclusion, but not the overall one, which is the final sentence; C describes the 'It is true that' sentence, and D reverses the direction of support between the principle and the sonnet example.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The conditions under which serialized novels were produced don't by themselves show those novels lack artistic merit.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Constraints aren't inherently opposed to artistry (intermediate conclusion); the sonnet's fourteen lines are a constraint, yet sonnets can be art.

breakdown.analysis: Map the support: sonnet analogy → 'constraints aren't inherently opposed to artistry' → 'Thus' serialized novels' conditions don't show lack of merit. The claim in question gets support (from the sonnet) and gives support (to the final sentence). That's an intermediate conclusion. Lesson: a claim can be both supported and supporting; only the one at the end of the chain is the main conclusion.

choices.note: The main trap. It is a conclusion, supported by the sonnet case, but the argument's ultimate point is the 'Thus' sentence about serialized novels.
The critics argue the opposite. This claim is the author's, used against the critics.
That describes the 'It is true that' sentence about serial constraints. The claim here begins with 'But' and pushes back against the critics.
Backwards. The sonnet example supports the general principle; the principle isn't there to illustrate the sonnet.
CORRECT. The sonnet analogy supports it, and it in turn supports the main conclusion that serial-publication conditions don't by themselves show a lack of artistic merit.

questions.stimulus: Nutrition researcher: Advocates of the Brannock diet claim that it lowers blood pressure, and they cite a twelve-week trial in support. But although participants in that trial who followed the diet showed a small average reduction in blood pressure, the reduction was too small to be statistically significant. So, contrary to its advocates' claims, the Brannock diet does not lower blood pressure.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the nutrition researcher's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: attacks the advocates of the diet rather than addressing the evidence that they cite
treats the failure of a study to establish that an effect exists as establishing that the effect does not exist
infers that the diet is ineffective for everyone from evidence that it was ineffective for most participants
relies on a trial that the diet's own advocates have cited as support for their position
presumes that lowering blood pressure is the only health benefit that advocates claim for the diet
questions.explanation: A non-significant result means only that the trial failed to show an effect, not that there is none, yet the researcher concludes the diet does not lower blood pressure; B describes this. C is the tempting trap, but the argument never relies on a claim about 'most participants' and generalizes from no such subgroup; D describes something that is not a flaw, since using an opponent's own evidence is legitimate, and E is wrong because the conclusion concerns only blood pressure.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Brannock diet does not lower blood pressure.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a 12-week trial, the diet's followers had a small average reduction in blood pressure that wasn't statistically significant.

breakdown.analysis: A non-significant result means the trial didn't prove an effect. It doesn't prove there's no effect. Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence, especially when the trial actually showed a small drop. It's like failing to find your keys in a quick search and concluding you don't own keys. The researcher could say 'the trial doesn't support the claim,' but not 'the diet doesn't work.'

choices.note: The researcher addresses the trial evidence directly; there's no attack on the advocates themselves.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The diet's advocates sell cookbooks, so their claims about blood pressure are worthless.

choices.note: CORRECT. The trial failed to establish that the diet lowers blood pressure, and the researcher treats that as showing the diet doesn't lower it.
The tempting trap, but the argument never mentions 'most participants' or a subgroup. It reasons from the average result.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The diet didn't work for most people in the trial, so it doesn't work for anyone.

choices.note: Using your opponents' own evidence against them is perfectly legitimate. Not a flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The advocates cited this trial, so it must be biased in their favor.

choices.note: The conclusion is only about blood pressure. The argument makes no assumption about other benefits.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The diet doesn't lower blood pressure, so it has no health benefits at all.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, populations of purple sea urchins off the coast of Velmar have exploded, and the urchins have stripped large areas of the kelp forests on which they feed. During the same decade, the number of sunflower sea stars, which are major predators of urchins, fell sharply in the area because of a wasting disease. Marine biologists conclude that the loss of the sea stars is the main cause of the urchin population explosion.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the biologists' argument?
choices: Purple sea urchins can survive long periods without food by sharply reducing their metabolism.
Water temperatures off Velmar rose during the decade, and warmer water increases urchin larval survival.
Sunflower sea stars off Velmar prefer purple sea urchins to every other prey species available to them.
In a nearby bay that the disease never reached, urchin numbers changed little despite similar water conditions.
The kelp forests off Velmar provide habitat for many fish species in addition to sea urchins.
questions.explanation: D supplies a controlled comparison: where the predator survived under similar conditions, urchins did not explode, which supports singling out the predator's loss as the main cause. C is the tempting trap: it bolsters the premise that sea stars prey on urchins but does nothing to rule out other causes or show the loss was the main cause. B offers a rival cause and weakens the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The loss of sunflower sea stars is the main cause of the purple urchin explosion off Velmar.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Urchin numbers exploded over the decade; in the same decade, sea stars, a major urchin predator, fell sharply due to disease.

breakdown.analysis: Two things happened at the same time, so one caused the other. The gap: maybe something else (warmer water, less fishing of other predators) drove the explosion. Best strengthener: a comparison where the predator survived and nothing else differed. If urchins didn't explode there, the predator loss looks like the real cause. That's a natural control group.

choices.note: Explains how urchins survive after stripping kelp, but says nothing about why their numbers exploded.
A rival cause. Warmer water boosting larval survival could explain the explosion, so this weakens.
The tempting trap. It shows sea stars really like urchins, bolstering the premise, but it doesn't rule out other causes or show the sea star loss was the main cause.
CORRECT. A nearby bay with similar water conditions but no disease saw little change in urchins. That isolates the sea star loss as the key difference and supports it as the main cause.
Kelp's value for fish is about why the problem matters, not about what caused the urchin explosion.

questions.stimulus: No student may join the debate team's traveling squad unless he or she is enrolled in the honors rhetoric course, and only students whose grade-point average is above 3.5 may enroll in honors rhetoric. Some members of the Corbin High debate team who are juniors are on the traveling squad. So some juniors on the Corbin High debate team have a grade-point average above 3.5.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Only paintings that have been restored can be displayed in the east wing, and every restored painting has been insured. All of the museum's Dutch paintings are displayed in the east wing. So all of the museum's Dutch paintings have been insured.

No bread may be labeled artisanal unless it is shaped by hand, and only bakeries with stone ovens shape bread by hand. Some of the Linden Bakery's breads are shaped by hand. So some of the Linden Bakery's breads are labeled artisanal.

A trail in Kessel Park can be opened to cyclists only if it has been resurfaced, and no trail is resurfaced unless it is wider than two meters. Some of the park's lakeside trails are open to cyclists. So some of the park's lakeside trails are wider than two meters.

Only licensed electricians may install the panels, and only people who have completed the safety course may be licensed. Some workers at the site have completed the safety course. So some workers at the site may install the panels.
Some vessels in the harbor are tankers, and only vessels with double hulls may carry crude oil. Every tanker in the harbor has a double hull. So some vessels in the harbor carry crude oil.
questions.explanation: The original is valid: being on the squad requires honors rhetoric, which requires a GPA above 3.5; some juniors are on the squad, so some juniors meet the GPA requirement. C chains two necessary conditions the same way and draws the same 'some' conclusion. A is the trap: it is also valid, but it reasons from an 'all' premise to an 'all' conclusion, so its pattern differs; B and D reverse necessary conditions, and E treats a necessary condition as sufficient.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some juniors on the debate team have a GPA above 3.5.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Traveling squad → honors rhetoric; honors rhetoric → GPA above 3.5; some juniors are on the traveling squad.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A → B; B → C; some D are A; so some D are C.

breakdown.analysis: Valid chain. Squad → honors → GPA > 3.5. Some juniors are on the squad, so those juniors have GPA > 3.5. Look for an answer with two linked necessary conditions (worded with 'only' or 'unless'), a 'some' premise that triggers the start of the chain, and a 'some' conclusion about the end.

choices.note: The trap. It's valid too, but it uses an 'all' premise to get an 'all' conclusion. The original uses 'some' to get 'some.' Different pattern.
Reverses the chain. Artisanal → shaped by hand, but being shaped by hand doesn't make bread artisanal. 'Some are hand-shaped, so some are artisanal' goes backwards.
CORRECT. Open to cyclists → resurfaced → wider than 2 meters. Some lakeside trails are open to cyclists, so some lakeside trails are wider than 2 meters. Same structure, same 'some' conclusion.
Reversed. Install → licensed → safety course. Having completed the safety course is the end of the chain; you can't run it backwards to 'may install.'
Treats a necessary condition as sufficient. A double hull is required to carry crude oil, but having one doesn't mean a vessel carries crude.

questions.stimulus: Fishery managers in Orrin Sound plan to help the declining stock of silver croaker recover by banning commercial croaker fishing during the species' spawning months. But the ban will do little to help the stock. The great majority of the croaker caught commercially in Orrin Sound are taken as unintended bycatch by shrimp trawlers, and the ban does not apply to shrimp trawling.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: A substantial amount of shrimp trawling in Orrin Sound takes place during the croaker's spawning months.
Shrimp trawlers in Orrin Sound could not easily be modified to reduce the amount of croaker bycatch.
The decline of the silver croaker stock has been caused primarily by pollution rather than by fishing.
The fishery managers lack the legal authority to impose restrictions on shrimp trawling.
Recreational anglers in Orrin Sound catch more croaker each year than commercial fishers do.
questions.explanation: The ban covers only the spawning months; if little shrimp trawling happened then, the croaker caught in those months would come mainly from directed fishing, which the ban removes, so the argument needs A. C and E are the tempting traps: each would make the ban look less useful, but the argument's reasoning rests on bycatch and does not depend on them; B and D concern what else might be done, not whether this ban helps.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The spawning-month ban on commercial croaker fishing will do little to help the croaker stock.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most commercially caught croaker are taken as bycatch by shrimp trawlers; the ban doesn't apply to shrimp trawling.

breakdown.analysis: The ban only covers spawning months. The bycatch statistic is about the year as a whole. If shrimp trawlers barely operate during spawning months, then during those months most croaker deaths would come from directed fishing, exactly what the ban stops. So the argument needs shrimp trawling to actually happen during spawning months. It's like saying a weekend speed camera won't help because most speeding happens on commuter routes, without checking whether commuters drive on weekends.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: little shrimp trawling happens during spawning months. Then in those months, the croaker catch is mostly directed fishing, which the ban removes, so the ban could help a lot. The argument collapses. Required.
choices.negation: Little shrimp trawling in Orrin Sound takes place during the croaker's spawning months.

choices.note: Negate it: trawlers could easily be modified. That's about what else managers could do, not whether this ban helps. The argument stands.
choices.negation: Shrimp trawlers in Orrin Sound could easily be modified to reduce the amount of croaker bycatch.

choices.note: Tempting because it would make the ban look less useful. But negate it: pollution isn't the main cause. The argument's bycatch reasoning still works fine. Not required.
choices.negation: The decline of the silver croaker stock has not been caused primarily by pollution rather than by fishing.

choices.note: Negate it: managers do have authority over trawling. That doesn't change whether this particular ban helps.
choices.negation: The fishery managers have the legal authority to impose restrictions on shrimp trawling.

choices.note: Another tempting add-on. Negate it: recreational anglers catch less than commercial fishers. The argument didn't rely on recreational catch at all.
choices.negation: Recreational anglers in Orrin Sound do not catch more croaker each year than commercial fishers do.

questions.stimulus: Every claim exceeding $50,000 under a Larkfield Insurance homeowner's policy is reviewed by a senior adjuster, and every claim reviewed by a senior adjuster is audited by Larkfield's compliance office. The compliance office audits no claim involving a property located outside the state unless the claim was filed under a commercial policy, and no homeowner's policy is a commercial policy. Some of Larkfield's homeowner's policies cover properties located outside the state.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
choices: Some claims audited by Larkfield's compliance office are for amounts of $50,000 or less.
Some claims reviewed by Larkfield's senior adjusters involve properties located outside the state.
Some homeowner's claims involving properties outside the state have been filed with Larkfield.
Some claims reviewed by Larkfield's senior adjusters were not filed under homeowner's policies.
Some claims exceeding $50,000 under Larkfield homeowner's policies involve properties outside the state.
questions.explanation: A homeowner's claim over $50,000 is reviewed by a senior adjuster and so audited; but an out-of-state claim can be audited only if it was filed under a commercial policy, which a homeowner's policy never is, so E is impossible. B is the trap: out-of-state claims filed under commercial policies can be audited, so senior adjusters may well have reviewed some; A, C, and D are each consistent with the statements.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Homeowner's claim over $50,000 → reviewed by senior adjuster; 2) reviewed by senior adjuster → audited; 3) audited AND out-of-state property → commercial policy; 4) homeowner's policy → NOT commercial; 5) some homeowner's policies cover out-of-state properties.

breakdown.analysis: Follow a homeowner's claim over $50,000 on an out-of-state property. Over $50,000 → reviewed → audited. Audited and out-of-state → must be commercial. But homeowner's policies are never commercial. Contradiction. So no such claim can exist. That's what CANNOT be true.

choices.note: Nothing says only claims over $50,000 are audited. Smaller claims could be reviewed and audited too. Could be true.
The trap. Out-of-state claims under commercial policies can be audited, so senior adjusters could have reviewed them. Could be true.
Fine, as long as these claims are $50,000 or less (so they don't get pushed into an audit). Could be true.
Senior adjusters could review commercial claims too. Nothing limits their reviews to homeowner's policies. Could be true.
CORRECT. A homeowner's claim over $50,000 must be reviewed and then audited. An audited out-of-state claim must be commercial, and homeowner's policies never are. So this combination is impossible.

questions.stimulus: Pilots at Corvane Air who completed the airline's new simulator-based course on recovering from sudden wind shear were later rated by flight examiners as substantially more skilled at wind-shear recovery than were pilots who had completed the older classroom-based course. The airline's training director concludes that the simulator course is the more effective way to teach wind-shear recovery and plans to discontinue the classroom course.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the training director's argument?
choices: The simulator-based course costs the airline considerably more per pilot than the classroom course does.
Examiners rated all pilots in the same simulator used in the new course, a device only its graduates had flown.
Pilots in the classroom course were taught by instructors with more years of experience than the simulator instructors had.
Wind shear encountered in actual flight differs in a few respects from the wind shear reproduced in simulators.
Pilots were assigned to one course or the other on a random basis by the airline's scheduling office.
questions.explanation: If skill was measured in the very simulator the new course used, its graduates may have scored better simply from familiarity with the device, so the ratings may not reflect superior recovery skill; B undermines the evidence itself. D is the strongest trap: it questions how well simulators mirror real flight, but nothing says the ratings were done in a simulator, and slight differences would not explain the gap between the groups. C actually makes the simulator course's success more impressive, and E strengthens the argument by ruling out self-selection.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The simulator course is the more effective way to teach wind-shear recovery; the classroom course should be discontinued.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Examiners rated simulator-course pilots substantially more skilled at wind-shear recovery than classroom-course pilots.

breakdown.analysis: What if the test itself favors one group? If skill was measured in the same simulator the new course used, those pilots had home-field advantage. They know the machine. Higher scores might reflect familiarity with the device, not better recovery skill. It's like giving a driving test in one student's own car and the other student's never-seen-before car.

choices.note: Cost doesn't affect which course teaches better. The conclusion is about effectiveness.
CORRECT. The test was in the very simulator only the new-course graduates had flown. Their higher ratings could be device familiarity, so the evidence doesn't show the course teaches recovery better.
Makes the simulator course's result more impressive: its graduates outperformed despite less experienced instructors. Doesn't weaken.
The strongest trap. Simulators being imperfect copies of real flight is a general worry, but 'a few respects' is minor, and it doesn't explain why one group scored much higher than the other.
Random assignment rules out the 'better pilots chose the simulator' worry. That strengthens.

questions.stimulus: Superintendent: Critics of our proposal to lengthen the school day argue that by mid-afternoon students are too tired to learn anything. But if that argument were sound, it would equally show that the afternoon classes our schools already hold are worthless. Yet these same critics have opposed every recent attempt to shorten the school day by cutting those afternoon classes. So the critics must either give up their argument or accept that afternoon instruction is worthless.
questions.stem: The superintendent's argument proceeds by
choices: offering evidence that students are not in fact too tired to learn in the afternoon
questioning the critics' motives for opposing the proposal to lengthen the school day
showing that the critics' conclusion is inconsistent with the evidence they cite for it
arguing that the critics' reasoning, if applied consistently, would commit them to a position they reject
showing that adopting the critics' conclusion would have consequences harmful to students
questions.explanation: The superintendent shows that the critics' reasoning implies afternoon classes are worthless, a position their own opposition to cutting those classes rejects; D describes this. C is the most tempting trap: the inconsistency alleged is between the critics' argument and their other positions, not between their conclusion and their evidence. E fails because no harm to students is claimed, and no evidence about fatigue is offered, ruling out A.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The critics must either give up their argument or accept that afternoon instruction is worthless.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: If students are too tired to learn by mid-afternoon, existing afternoon classes are worthless; yet the critics have opposed cutting those classes.

breakdown.analysis: The superintendent doesn't argue about fatigue at all. He takes the critics' reasoning, applies it to current afternoon classes, and shows it leads somewhere the critics themselves reject. It's like a friend who says 'it's too late to start a project after 3 p.m.' but always does homework at 4. This is a consistency attack, not a direct rebuttal.

choices.note: No evidence about fatigue is offered. The superintendent never says students aren't tired.
choices.example: Example of this method: Studies show students' test scores are just as high in afternoon classes, so they aren't too tired to learn.

choices.note: He doesn't question motives. He points out inconsistency in their positions.
choices.example: Example of this method: The critics oppose a longer day only because the teachers' union pays them, so ignore them.

choices.note: The most tempting trap. The inconsistency is between the critics' reasoning and another position they hold (opposing cuts), not between their conclusion and their own evidence.
choices.example: Example of this method: The critics say students are too tired in the afternoon, but the data they cite shows afternoon test scores are higher.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the critics apply their fatigue reasoning consistently, it implies afternoon classes are worthless, a position they reject by opposing cuts to those classes.
The superintendent doesn't claim the critics' conclusion would harm students.
choices.example: Example of this method: If we don't lengthen the day as critics want, students will fall behind and suffer.

questions.stimulus: Conservationist: The Penrill Valley wind farm should not be expanded. Although the existing turbines have caused few bird deaths, the proposed expansion area lies along the migratory route of the gray crane, a species whose global population numbers fewer than two thousand. Even a handful of collisions a year could threaten the species' survival. Moreover, the electricity the expansion would provide could be generated at other available sites that pose no comparable risk to any species.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the conservationist's reasoning?
choices: An energy project should be expanded only if it has a record of causing few deaths among wild birds.
A project should not proceed if its benefits could be obtained at other sites at no greater financial cost.
A project should not proceed if it could threaten a species' survival and its benefits are obtainable elsewhere without such risk.
The survival of an endangered species should always take precedence over the economic interests of local residents.
A project that has caused little environmental harm so far should be presumed safe to expand unless new evidence emerges.
questions.explanation: The conservationist cites a threat to the crane's survival and the availability of alternative sites without such risk; C makes exactly those two facts sufficient for rejecting the expansion. B is the subtle trap: the argument says nothing about whether the other sites are equally cheap, so B's condition is not shown to be met. A's condition is satisfied by the farm's record and so cannot support opposing expansion, and D concerns economic interests the argument never mentions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Penrill Valley wind farm should not be expanded.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The expansion area is on the migratory route of the gray crane (under 2,000 birds); even a few collisions a year could threaten its survival; the electricity could be generated at other sites with no comparable risk.

breakdown.analysis: Two key facts: threatens a species' survival, and the benefit is available elsewhere without that risk. The ideal principle: if a project could threaten a species' survival AND its benefits can be had elsewhere without that risk → don't proceed. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, and its conditions must be met by the facts.

choices.note: Gives a requirement for expanding (few bird deaths), which the farm's current record meets. It can't justify opposing expansion.
The subtle trap. Its condition is 'no greater financial cost.' The conservationist never says the other sites are equally cheap, so we can't tell the condition is met.
CORRECT. The expansion could threaten the crane's survival, and the electricity could be generated elsewhere without such risk. Both conditions met → don't proceed. Exactly the conclusion.
The argument never mentions local residents' economic interests. And it's not clear the crane is officially 'endangered.' Off target.
Pushes toward expansion, the opposite of the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Literary critic: Readers who say they enjoy Tomas Hellen's poetry most often explain that they find it consoling. But consolation is not an aesthetic response; after all, one can be consoled by a greeting card or by a friend's kind words, neither of which need have any artistic merit. It follows that these readers' enjoyment of Hellen's poetry is not an aesthetic response to it.
questions.stem: The literary critic's argument is flawed in that it
choices: takes for granted that readers who find a poem consoling cannot also be responding to its aesthetic qualities
fails to establish that readers of Hellen's poetry are never consoled by greeting cards
relies on the reports of readers who may lack the expertise needed to evaluate poetry
infers that a property shared by some consoling objects is shared by all consoling objects
presumes that greeting cards and kind words have no aesthetic qualities whatsoever
questions.explanation: That readers mention consolation does not show that consolation is the whole of their enjoyment; they could be consoled and also respond to the poems' artistry, which the argument ignores, as A says. D is the most tempting trap: the argument does not infer that Hellen's poems lack artistic merit because greeting cards do; it uses the examples only to show that consolation can occur without art, which is legitimate. C fails because the argument relies on readers only for reports of their own reactions, and E overstates the examples, which say only that they 'need' have no merit.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Readers' enjoyment of Hellen's poetry is not an aesthetic response.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Those readers most often say they find the poetry consoling; consolation isn't an aesthetic response, since greeting cards and kind words console without needing artistic merit.

breakdown.analysis: Being consoled isn't, in itself, an aesthetic response. Fine. But that doesn't mean the readers aren't also responding aesthetically. People can find a song comforting AND think it's beautifully written. The critic assumes consolation is the whole of their enjoyment, which is an either/or that doesn't exist.

choices.note: CORRECT. The critic assumes that because readers find the poems consoling, their enjoyment can't also involve the poems' aesthetic qualities. Those two can coexist.
Whether these readers are consoled by greeting cards is irrelevant. The cards just show consolation can happen without art.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: You say greeting cards never console you, but you haven't proven it, so they must.

choices.note: The argument relies on readers only to report their own reactions. You don't need expertise to know whether you feel consoled.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Casual readers say the poem is technically masterful, so it must be.

choices.note: The most tempting trap. The argument doesn't say Hellen's poems lack merit because greeting cards do. It just uses cards to show consolation can occur without art, which is legitimate.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Greeting cards console people and have no artistic merit, so any consoling poem has no artistic merit.

choices.note: The argument only says these items 'need' have no merit, a much weaker claim. It doesn't presume they have no aesthetic qualities at all.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Greeting cards are mass-produced, so none of them can have any aesthetic quality.

questions.stimulus: Under the Fendale city charter, no budget item that would increase the city's annual spending by more than 2 percent can take effect unless it is approved in a public referendum. Referendums may be held only in months in which Fendale holds a general election, and Fendale holds general elections only in months in which the state also holds a general election. The proposed transit expansion would increase Fendale's annual spending by 3 percent. Therefore, the transit expansion will not take effect before next November.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion of the argument to be properly drawn?
choices: Fendale voters have rejected most past referendums on items that would increase city spending.
In every month in which the state holds a general election, Fendale also holds a general election.
No referendum on the transit expansion has yet been scheduled by the Fendale city council.
Neither Fendale nor the state has held a general election at any time during the past twelve months.
The state will not hold a general election at any time before next November.
questions.explanation: Taking effect requires referendum approval, a referendum requires a Fendale election month, and a Fendale election month requires a state election month; if the state holds no election before next November, the expansion cannot take effect before then, so E suffices. B is the subtle trap: it reverses the final conditional and does nothing to rule out an early election; D concerns the past rather than the coming months, and C leaves open that a referendum could still be scheduled.

setup.label: Conclusion
