setup.text: The transit expansion will not take effect before next November.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Increase over 2% → needs referendum approval; referendum → Fendale general election month; Fendale election → state general election month; the expansion increases spending 3%.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: takes effect → referendum → Fendale election month → state election month. Contrapositive: no state election → no Fendale election → no referendum → can't take effect. So if the state holds no general election before next November, the expansion can't take effect before then. That's the missing piece.

choices.note: Past rejections don't guarantee a future rejection, and it says nothing about timing.
The subtle trap. Reverses the last conditional (state election → Fendale election). It doesn't rule out an early election, so it can't block early approval.
No referendum scheduled yet doesn't mean none can be held before November. A referendum could still be scheduled for an upcoming election month.
About the past twelve months, not the coming months. An election next month would still let the referendum happen.
CORRECT. No state election before November → no Fendale election → no referendum → expansion can't take effect before November. Conclusion locked.

questions.stimulus: Nutritionist: Parents often assume that a cereal's marketing tells them little about its contents. But consider the cereal aisle at Grantham Market. Most of the breakfast cereals sold there are high in added sugar, and most foods that are high in added sugar are marketed primarily to children. So most of the breakfast cereals sold at Grantham Market are marketed primarily to children.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the nutritionist's argument?
choices: Most of the novels in the Pell Library are hardcover, and all of the library's hardcover books are shelved on the second floor. So most of the library's novels are shelved on the second floor.
Most of the members of the Ridgeline Hiking Club live in Ardley, and most residents of Ardley own a car. So most of the members of the Ridgeline Hiking Club own a car.
Most of the trees in the Sorrel orchard are apple trees, and most of the orchard's apple trees were planted before 1990. So some of the trees in the orchard were planted before 1990.
Most of the paintings in the Vance Gallery are oil paintings, and some oil paintings are on canvas. So some of the paintings in the Vance Gallery are on canvas.
Most of the students in the poetry seminar are history majors, and most history majors at the college take Latin. So most students who take Latin are in the poetry seminar.
questions.explanation: The nutritionist chains two 'most' statements into a 'most' conclusion, which is invalid because the sugary cereals could fall among the minority of sugary foods not marketed to children; B makes exactly this move with club members and Ardley car owners. D is the strongest trap: it is flawed too, but it uses a 'some' premise and a 'some' conclusion, a different pattern; E commits a different error by reversing terms, and A and C are valid.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most breakfast cereals sold at Grantham Market are marketed primarily to children.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most cereals sold there are high in added sugar; most high-sugar foods are marketed primarily to children.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; most B are C; so most A are C.

breakdown.analysis: Same broken chain as always: two 'mosts' don't link. High-sugar foods are a huge category (candy, soda, pastries). The majority marketed to kids could be candy and soda, while the sugary cereals at Grantham all sit in the minority aimed at adults. Find the answer that stacks two 'mosts' into a 'most' conclusion with the terms in the same order.

choices.note: Valid. Most novels are hardcover, and ALL hardcovers are on the second floor, so most novels are on the second floor. The 'all' makes it work, so it doesn't match a flawed argument.

CORRECT. Most club members live in Ardley; most Ardley residents own a car; so most club members own a car. Same most-most-most chain, same flaw: the club members could all be in Ardley's car-free minority.
Valid. Most trees are apple trees, and most of those were planted before 1990, so at least some trees were planted before 1990. A 'some' conclusion from that is safe.
The strongest trap. It's flawed (the canvas oil paintings could all be elsewhere), but the pattern is most + some → some, not most + most → most.
A different error: it reverses the terms in the conclusion ('most Latin students are in the seminar'). The original keeps the direction A → C.

questions.stimulus: At Kestrel Field airport, most collisions between aircraft and birds occur during takeoff and landing. Over the past five years the airport has removed much of the grassland around its runways, which had attracted ground-feeding birds such as starlings, and collisions involving starlings have fallen substantially. Yet the total number of bird collisions at the airport rose slightly over that period. The number of collisions involving each other species except gulls, which feed at a landfill near the airport, remained roughly constant.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Removing grassland around the runways at Kestrel Field made the airport more attractive to gulls.
Collisions involving gulls at Kestrel Field now outnumber collisions involving starlings there.
The landfill near Kestrel Field has grown larger over the past five years.
The number of collisions involving gulls at Kestrel Field rose by more than the number involving starlings fell.
Removing grassland near runways does not reduce the overall number of bird collisions at airports.
questions.explanation: Starling collisions fell, every other species except gulls held roughly constant, and the total still rose, so gull collisions must have risen by more than starling collisions fell: D. B is the subtle trap: a gull increase larger than the starling decrease says nothing about whether gulls now outnumber starlings, since the starting numbers are unknown. A posits an unsupported causal link, and E overgeneralizes from one airport.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Most bird collisions happen at takeoff and landing; 2) grassland removal cut starling collisions substantially; 3) total collisions rose slightly over five years; 4) collisions for every other species except gulls stayed roughly constant.

breakdown.analysis: Do the bookkeeping. Starlings went down. Everyone else except gulls stayed flat. Yet the total went up. The only species left to account for the increase is gulls, and they had to rise enough to cover the starling drop and then some. Numbers: starlings −30, others 0, total +5 → gulls must be about +35.

choices.note: The facts don't link grassland removal to gulls. The gulls feed at a landfill. This adds a causal story the facts don't support.
The subtle trap. Gulls rose more than starlings fell, but we don't know the starting numbers. If starlings began at 200 and gulls at 20, gulls could still be well behind.
Possible explanation for more gull collisions, but nothing in the facts supports a bigger landfill. You can't pick an answer on a possibility.
CORRECT. Starling collisions fell, other species held steady, gulls are the only remaining variable, and the total still rose. So the gull increase must exceed the starling decrease.
Overgeneralizes from one airport to all airports, and even at Kestrel Field the removal did reduce starling collisions; the rise came from gulls.
